items.title: One year on, House of Faith has given Christian stories a free home on the world’s screens
items.description: House of Faith, the non-profit, faith-driven media organisation with offices in Lagos and London, today marks its first anniversary. In just one year, it has built FaithStream, Africa’s premier faith-based streaming platform, into a free global home for Christian stories, and moved from licensing films to making its own. Twelve months after its rollout, the Non-profit media organisation behind FaithStream marks its first anniversary with a free global streaming platform, more than 150 titles and its first original film that drew around 80,000 watch hours within hours. Next, this media and entertainment organisation takes Christian storytelling beyond film; we expect to see A House of Faith birth expressions in music, live events and more. Why it matters Turn on any screen and the stories are almost all secular. Families who want entertainment that reflects their faith, without a sermon and without a subscription fee, have had few places to look. Faith-based storytelling has too often been left at the edges of mainstream entertainment, underfunded, hard to find and harder to afford. House of Faith was founded on 26 November 2025 by Kunle Falodun and Hakeem Condotti to change that. Its mission is “…to increase the share of voice of Christian content in the world’s mainstream entertainment pool, anywhere the stories, the talent and the audience can be found.” A year of firsts Three months after its rollout, on 27 February 2026, House of Faith launched its flagship product, FaithStream, in Lagos. The platform removed the two biggest barriers to access. It is free to every user, funded entirely by donations and grants. And it is built for the way global audiences actually consume content: mobile-first, with offline downloads and adaptive streaming for every kind of connection, on iOS, Android and the web. In the nine months since, FaithStream’s library has grown to more than 150 titles, spanning feature films, series, podcasts and devotionals, with more in the works. On 20 November 2026, House of Faith released its first original film, Love & Porridge , a romantic comedy produced by LordTanner Studios and directed by Tolu “Lord Tanner” Awobiyi, starring Taye Arimoro, Wendy Lawal, Michael Ejoor and Doris Okorie. Free and exclusive to FaithStream, it recorded around 80,000 watch hours within hours of going live worldwide. No one paid a subscription to watch. The response was not bought; it was earned by a story people wanted to see. The people behind the year House of Faith’s first year belongs to the filmmakers who trusted it with their stories, the cast and crews who brought them to life, the donors and partners who keep every title free, and the viewers across Africa and its diaspora who pressed play on every kind of connection, and told their friends. “A year ago, we started House of Faith with one conviction: Christian stories deserve a place at the centre of entertainment, not at its edges. In twelve months, we launched FaithStream, built a library of more than 150 titles and released our first original, and audiences answered within hours. Africa has the stories, the talent and the audience. Our job is to give them a home, and this is only our first year.” Kunle Falodun, Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder, House of Faith “We built FaithStream so that no one is left out: no subscription, no fast connection required, just press play. Every viewer this year proves that when you remove the barriers, people come. Our job now is to reach the next million.” Hakeem Condotti, Chief Product Officer and Co-founder, House of Faith What comes next FaithStream is House of Faith’s first product, not its last. Going into its second year, House of Faith will roll out new projects and products that spread and deepen the reach of Christian content across film, music, entertainment and media. It is developing production studios in Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa, alongside pan-African television distribution, publishing and live events. The aim is unchanged: to increase the share of voice of Christian content in the world’s secular entertainment, with stories good enough to stand beside anything else people are watching. House of Faith: year one at a glance House of Faith rolled out House of Faith launched in London, United Kingdom, on the 26th November 2025. Founders Kunle Falodun (CEO) and Hakeem Condotti (Chief Product Officer) Offices Lagos, London, America Flagship product FaithStream, launched globally in Lagos on 27 February 2026 FaithStream library More than 150 titles: feature films, series, podcasts and devotionals First original Love & Porridge , Premiered 6th November, released 20 November 2026 Opening response Around 80,000 watch hours within hours of release Price to viewers Free; the platform is funded by donations and grants Built for Mobile-first viewing, offline downloads, adaptive streaming Available on iOS, Android and the web at thefaithstream.com (TV App coming soon) In development Production studios in Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa; pan-African TV distribution, publishing and live events Be part of year two House of Faith’s work stays free because people choose to stand with it. There are four ways to be a part of this mission: Give. Every gift keeps Christian films, series and stories free for anyone, anywhere. Donate at ahouseoffaith.org/pages/donate . Bring your story. Filmmakers and producers with faith-based stories are invited to discuss licensing and original production partnerships with House of Faith. Contact: ivy.of@ahouseoffaith.org Partner with us. Brands, foundations and grant-makers can help take Christian content into film, music, entertainment and media across Africa and the world. Contact: ivy.of@ahouseoffaith.org Press play. Watch Love & Porridge and more than 150 titles free on FaithStream. Download the app from the Apple App Store or Google Play, or watch at thefaithstream.com

items.title: Violences faites aux femmes : 60 % des femmes tuées en 2025 l’ont été par leur conjoint ou un proche
items.description: Le domicile reste le lieu le plus dangereux pour les femmes. En 2025, cinq femmes ont été tuées chaque heure dans le monde par leur partenaire intime ou un membre de leur famille, soit 129 victimes par jour. Au total, 60 % des quelque 78.000 meurtres de femmes enregistrés au cours de l’année ont été commis dans ce cercle familial ou conjugal. Ces chiffres figurent dans une note d’information des Nations unies consacrée aux meurtres de femmes et de filles, publiée à l’occasion de la Journée internationale pour l’élimination de la violence à l’égard des femmes. Le constat, qui se répète depuis plusieurs années, témoigne de la persistance d’un phénomène dont le domicile demeure le principal théâtre. Aucune région du monde n’est épargnée par les meurtres de femmes motivés par leur genre, relève le document onusien. L’Afrique affiche le taux le plus élevé de femmes tuées par leur partenaire intime ou un membre de leur famille, avec 2,9 victimes pour 100.000 femmes. Les Amériques arrivent en deuxième position, avec 1,4 victime, devant l’Océanie (1,1), l’Asie (0,6) et l’Europe (0,5). Pour Monica Juma, directrice exécutive de l’Office des Nations unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC), la persistance de ces statistiques alarmantes traduit l’enracinement de facteurs sociaux et institutionnels qui favorisent les violences. Les attitudes collectives, les normes sociales préjudiciables et l’insuffisance des mécanismes institutionnels de protection contribuent à instaurer un climat dans lequel le meurtre d’une épouse, d’une fille, d’une mère ou d’une sœur peut être perçu comme tolérable, a-t-elle déploré. La responsable onusienne appelle à une mobilisation durable de l’ensemble de la société. Elle préconise notamment de renforcer les stratégies de prévention afin de faire évoluer les comportements et de combattre les attitudes sociales néfastes. Elle insiste également sur la nécessité d’investir dans des programmes spécialisés destinés à prendre en charge les auteurs de violences domestiques, tout en renforçant la protection des femmes et le respect de leurs droits fondamentaux et de leur dignité. Le rapport rappelle que les féminicides surviennent rarement de manière isolée. Pour de nombreuses femmes et filles, ils constituent l’ultime épisode d’un continuum de violences, de menaces et de mauvais traitements qui aurait pu être interrompu. Pourtant, la majorité des victimes de violences physiques ou sexuelles ne sollicitent pas l’aide de leurs proches, de leur communauté ou des autorités, en raison des nombreux obstacles auxquels elles sont confrontées. Une situation qui laisse de nombreuses femmes sans protection et permet aux auteurs de violences d’échapper durablement à toute forme de responsabilité ou de sanction. Face à cette réalité, Sima Bahous, directrice exécutive d’ONU Femmes, plaide pour que les femmes et les filles puissent signaler les violences sans mettre leur sécurité en danger, accéder à une protection effective et bénéficier d'un accompagnement avant qu’il ne soit trop tard. Elle met en garde contre les conséquences potentiellement mortelles de l’absence de signalement des signes précurseurs, du manque de diligence des autorités dans le traitement des affaires et de l’insuffisance des dispositifs de protection et de poursuite judiciaire. Chaque occasion manquée de garantir la sécurité des femmes et des filles constitue, selon elle, un échec de la justice et un manquement à l’une des obligations fondamentales du droit : protéger leur vie. D’où son appel à une action urgente pour qu’aucun signal d’alerte ne soit négligé, qu’aucune survivante de violences ne soit laissée sans protection et qu’aucun auteur ne puisse se soustraire à ses responsabilités. La baisse générale des homicides ne se traduit pas par une diminution équivalente des féminicides. Le rapport souligne en effet un décalage dans l’évolution de ces deux phénomènes. Entre 2010 et 2025, le taux global d’homicides a diminué de 23 % dans les Amériques, alors que celui des meurtres de femmes liés au genre n’a reculé que de 12 %. En Europe, le contraste est également marqué : le taux d’homicides a baissé de 43 %, contre 28 % pour les féminicides. La publication de ces données intervient dans le cadre de la campagne annuelle des « 16 jours d’activisme contre la violence basée sur le genre », organisée du 25 novembre au 10 décembre. L’édition de cette année est placée sous le thème : « Unissons-nous pour mettre fin aux violences contre les femmes et les filles : faire respecter la justice, protéger les survivantes et mettre fin à l’impunité ». À cette occasion, ONU Femmes et l’ONUDC appellent les gouvernements, le secteur privé, le système des Nations unies, les médias, les organisations féminines ainsi que les survivantes engagées dans la conduite du changement à coordonner leurs efforts. L’objectif est de mettre un terme aux féminicides et à toutes les formes de violence contre les femmes et les filles, de garantir l’accès à la justice aux survivantes, aux victimes et à leurs proches, et de faire en sorte que les auteurs de ces crimes répondent de leurs actes. The post Violences faites aux femmes : 60 % des femmes tuées en 2025 l’ont été par leur conjoint ou un proche appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Le Sénégal inaugure son troisième site aurifère à Boto
items.description: Le Sénégal compte désormais trois mines industrielles d’or, avec l’entrée en exploitation du site de Boto, dans la commune de Médina Baffé, après Sabodala et Mako. Le Président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, a procédé, ce jeudi, à l’inauguration de cette nouvelle infrastructure minière portée par le groupe MANAGEM. Selon les informations de la communication de la Présidence de la République, le projet représente «un investissement de près de 464 millions de dollars, soit plus de 270 milliards de francs CFA. Il devrait générer environ 1 850 emplois directs et indirects et rapporter à l’État plus de 1 200 milliards de francs CFA sur toute la durée de son exploitation». Le Chef de l’État a notamment insisté sur la nécessité de faire du développement minier un véritable levier d’amélioration des conditions de vie des communautés locales. À cet effet, il a rappelé les instruments devant accompagner cette ambition, notamment « le nouveau Code minier, le contenu local, la transformation sur place et la mobilisation effective des fonds destinés aux collectivités ». « Le développement de Kédougou n'est ni une faveur ni une concession », a affirmé le Président de la République, rapporte la même source. items.title: Le Niger sur Kalangou du 26 novembre 2026
items.description: Listen to « Environnement, lutte traditionnelle (le Niger sur Kalangou) » on Spreaker. Dans l'emission de ce jeudi: dans la premiere partie, Moussa Kailou, directeur regional de l'environnement de Dosso, revient sur l'histoire de leur presence au Niger, notamment dans la zone de Koure, situee a environ 60 kilometres au sud-est de Niamey. Cette zone accueille une grande partie des girafes, qui evoluent a proximite des villages et des champs agricoles. Dans la seconde partie, Moussa Kailou explique que les deplacements de ces animaux s'inscrivent dans leur aire naturelle de repartition. Il apporte notamment des precisions sur l'apparition recente de plusieurs girafes a Kara-Kara, dans le departement de Tibiri, region de Dosso. Il repond aux questions d'Aoussi Abdourahamane. L'echo des regions nous conduit a Zinder, ou la lutte traditionnelle connaît une reprise apres pres de huit annees de ralentissement. a cette occasion, Dan Gally Saley, directeur regional de la jeunesse, des sports et de la culture de Zinder, partage ses impressions dans un reportage d'Ali Keita. items.title: Housing Ministry warns directors against shortcuts, corruption
items.description: By John Alechenu ABUJA — The Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, Dr Shuaib Belgore, has urged directors and senior management staff to lead by example and uphold integrity, transparency and accountability in the discharge of their duties. Belgore, represented by the Director of the Special Projects Unit, Mr Olatunde Ajayi, gave the charge at an anti-corruption sensitisation workshop organised by the ministry’s Anti-Corruption and Transparency Unit (ACTU) for directors and senior management officials. He said the ministry occupied a strategic position in national development through its mandate of facilitating access to affordable housing and promoting sustainable urban infrastructure for millions of Nigerians. He noted that achieving this mandate required an unwavering commitment to integrity, transparency and accountability, particularly in policy implementation, contract administration and the allocation of public resources. According to him, the theme of the workshop went beyond a slogan, describing it as a call for personal responsibility, ethical conduct and accountability, particularly among public servants entrusted with leadership positions. Belgore said directors, as heads of departments, played critical roles in institutional administration, workload approval, process supervision and mentoring of junior officers. He urged them to recognise that their actions, decisions and conduct set standards for the entire workforce, stressing that leadership must be demonstrated through personal example rather than instructions alone. He said leaders who consistently demonstrated integrity and accountability would create an enabling environment for ethical conduct, institutional discipline and compliance with established regulations. The permanent secretary charged senior management officials to reject all forms of unethical practices, abuse of office and administrative shortcuts, while ensuring strict compliance with the Public Service Rules and the Public Procurement Act. ACTU seeks stronger ethical culture Earlier, the Head of ACTU, Umar Muhammed, said the participation of the management team demonstrated a collective commitment to the highest standards of integrity, accountability and transparency in public service. He said integrity was not merely a personal responsibility but an institutional obligation requiring responsible stewardship in the management of public resources. Muhammed noted that decisions taken by public officers and the examples they set influenced the ethical culture, institutional credibility and overall performance of the ministry. He explained that the workshop was designed to institutionalise ethical governance, strengthen internal control mechanisms and promote compliance with laws, policies and regulations guiding public service operations. Also delivering a goodwill message on behalf of the Chairman of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Dr Musa Adamu Aliyu, the Director of System Study and Review, Mr Olusegun Adigun, said the workshop reflected the ministry’s commitment to ethical values, accountability and responsible public service. He noted that the ministry’s policies and programmes had direct implications for economic growth, social stability and citizens’ welfare. Adigun stressed the need to entrench integrity in public administration to strengthen public confidence and ensure that resources were deployed for the benefit of Nigerians. The ACTU had earlier organised a similar sensitisation workshop for officers on Grade Level 15 and below as part of efforts to promote ethical standards across all cadres. The latest workshop forms part of the ministry’s broader efforts to deepen institutional accountability, promote ethical leadership and reinforce zero tolerance for corruption in the public service. The post Housing Ministry warns directors against shortcuts, corruption appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Grande Panda et Doblò Panorama : Fiat Algérie met en garde contre les arnaques
items.description: Lancée il y a à peine 72 heures par Fiat Algérie , la Grande Panda au même titre que Fiat Doblò Panorama laquelle connaît un succès commercial retentissant, fait déjà l'objet de tentatives d'arnaques. Devant cette situation, FIAT EL DJAZAIR lance l'alerte et appelle à la vigilance face à des pratiques frauduleuses qui pourraient coûter cher aux personnes ciblées. Arnaque à la Grande Panda : un « modus operandi » bien huilé En effet et dans un communiqué parvenu TSA, Fiat Algérie met en garde contre des personnes se faisant passer pour la marque ou pour des représentants de son réseau d’agents agréés afin de proposer l’acquisition de véhicules, notamment la Fiat Grande Panda et le Fiat Doblò Panorama. Ces individus, selon la même source, demandent aux clients de communiquer leurs identifiants, mots de passe, codes de sécurité ou coordonnées bancaires sous prétexte de faciliter leurs démarches. Fiat Algérie précise qu’il s’agit de tentatives de fraude et appelle à ne transmettre, en aucun cas, ces informations confidentielles. Les démarches officielles à suivre pour acheter une Fiat Grand Panda La marque rappelle que les inscriptions s'effectuent exclusivement sur son site officiel, www.fiat.dz . Elles sont entièrement gratuites, sans engagement et traitées par ordre chronologique. La finalisation de l'acquisition d'un véhicule se déroule uniquement en présentiel auprès d'un agent agréé de la marque italienne en Algérie. Aucune communication de données confidentielles n'est requise dans ce cadre. La liste des agents agréés est également disponible sur le site officiel. Un numéro pour signaler les fraudes En cas de doute ou de sollicitation suspecte, FIAT EL DJAZAIR invite ses clients à contacter directement son service client au 0770 165 165, afin de vérifier l'authenticité de toute démarche. Le constructeur appelle ainsi à la vigilance et recommande de privilégier exclusivement ses canaux officiels pour toute opération liée à l'acquisition de ses véhicules. items.title: Frontières de Guinée, du Mali et du Sénégal : le programme RéZo accélère sur la résilience et annonce 5 millions d’euros supplémentaires
items.description: Les délégations de la Guinée, du Mali et du Sénégal se sont réunies le mercredi 25 et jeudi 26 novembre 2026 dans un hôtel de Conakry à l'occasion du deuxième Comité de pilotage régional du programme « Renforcement de la Résilience dans les Zones frontalières » (RéZo). Un an après la première session tenue à Dakar en octobre 2025, cette rencontre rassemble les représentants des gouvernements, les instances en charge des frontières, l'Union européenne, l'Allemagne ainsi que les opérateurs de mise en œuvre, la GIZ, Coginta et le Centre pour le dialogue humanitaire (HD) afin d'évaluer les premiers acquis et de fixer les priorités communes pour 2027. A l'ouverture des travaux, Mme l'ambassadeur de la République fédérale d'Allemagne en Guinée, Irène Biontino, a salué les progrès rapides enregistrés dans 63 communes frontalières à travers les trois volets du programme (« RéZo Emploi et Services », « RéZo Coopération » et « Stabilité »). Elle a annoncé que l'Allemagne prévoit de prolonger son engagement et d'augmenter sa contribution de cinq (05) millions d'euros au profit des composantes « RéZo Emploi et Services » et « RéZo Coopération » mises en œuvre par la GIZ, afin de consolider la formation professionnelle, l'insertion économique et la réhabilitation d'infrastructures de base. De son côté, le représentant de la délégation de l'Union européenne en Guinée, M. Xavier Sticker, a rappelé l'investissement de 30 millions d'euros mobilisé par le budget européen aux côtés des financements allemands. Il a souligné la nécessité d'inscrire ces réalisations dans la durée et de transformer les zones frontalières en espaces de continuité et d'opportunités : « Il importe également que les infrastructures non seulement soient mises en place, inaugurées, mais qu'elles aient les moyens, les ressources pour fonctionner, pour pouvoir elles aussi s'inscrire dans la durée. » A fin octobre 2026, les bilans présentés font état de 43 infrastructures sociales de base réhabilitées, de plus de 2 500 jeunes et femmes formés sur les plans technique, professionnel et entrepreneurial, ainsi que de 585 000 personnes bénéficiant déjà d'un meilleur accès à l'eau, à l'électricité ou à l'éducation. Par ailleurs, 10 000 personnes profitent de meilleures conditions de revenus, un chiffre qui atteint 5 400 personnes dans les premières données de revenus évoquées en séance d'ouverture, tandis que la coopération a été renforcée entre plus de 200 acteurs et que la Semaine Tripartite organisée en Guinée en avril 2026 a rassemblé plus de 1 000 participants. Sur le plan de la coopération transfrontalière, l'officialisation en septembre 2026 du Groupement Local de Coopération Transfrontalière (GLCT) Ambidédi-Bakel-Sadiola, réunissant dix collectivités du Mali et du Sénégal, marque une avancée structurante, complétée par l'accompagnement des GLCT de Mandiana-Yanfolila et de Siguiri-Kangaba entre la Guinée et le Mali, ainsi que par la création attendue en décembre 2026 du GLCT Koundara-Salémata-Vélingara entre la Guinée et le Sénégal. Sur le volet stabilité, Coginta a notamment formé 211 gendarmes et 27 sous-préfets au Sénégal sur la sécurité et la gouvernance des territoires frontaliers, tandis que HD a accompagné au Mali une étude diagnostique sur les conflits et la signature de trois engagements communautaires pour une gestion apaisée des ressources naturelles dans les cercles de Sébécoro/Sby, Sagabari et Sélingué. Prenant la parole au nom du ministre malien de l'Administration Territoriale et de la Décentralisation (MATD), le conseiller technique M. Moussa Bilane a insisté sur la nécessité de privilégier les activités à impact transfrontalier et d'apporter des réponses conjointes sur des espaces tels que Madina-Yenfoula, Siguiri-Kankan, Diboli-Kayes-Sadiola, Kita et l'espace tripartite. Le président de la Commission Nationale de Gestion des Frontières (CNGF) du Sénégal, M. Aboubacar Camara, a pour sa part, a plaidé pour le renforcement des investissements structurants et la pérennisation des mécanismes de coopération : « Les frontières ne constituent pas seulement des limites territoriales. Elles sont des espaces de vie, d'échanges, de complémentarité économique et de cohésion sociale. » En déclarant ouverte cette deuxième session à Conakry, la ministre guinéenne de l'Administration du territoire et de la Décentralisation, Mme Camara Djénabou Touré a replacé l'action du programme dans la dynamique de gouvernance territoriale et du programme « Simandou 2040 », soulignant que les zones frontalières doivent devenir des passerelles de paix, de sécurité et de prospérité partagée. D'ici 2028, le programme RéZo poursuit trois grands objectifs dans les 63 communes frontalières : améliorer l'accès à l'eau, à l'électricité et à l'éducation pour 2 millions de personnes, contribuer à l'amélioration des revenus de 40 000 personnes principalement des jeunes et des femmes et renforcer la coopération entre plus de 1 000 acteurs.

items.title: Les délestages persistent dans plusieurs localités du Mali
items.description: Alors que la fourniture d'electricite connaît une amelioration a Bamako, la situation reste preoccupante dans certaines regions. a Douentza, Macina et Menaka, les coupures prolongees impactent les populations et portent un coup dur a leurs activites . Elles appellent les autorites a trouver des solutions durables a la crise energetique dans leurs localites. a Macina, dans la region de Segou, les delestages affectent de nombreuses activites economiques. Au-dela des pertes financieres, les consequences sur la securite et les conditions de vie des habitants inquietent egalement la societe civile. Moussa Dem, membre de cette organisation, alerte notamment sur les difficultes de conservation des produits alimentaires. « Sans electricite, l'insecurite peut augmenter. Les vendeurs de poissons et les bouchers ne peuvent plus conserver leurs produits au frais », explique-t-il. Il souligne egalement les consequences de ces coupures sur les activites des femmes en milieu rural, pour qui l'electricite constitue un outil de travail. Selon lui, cette situation favorise le chomage et penalise les activites generatrices de revenus. Il appelle les autorites a trouver des solutions, tout en reconnaissant que celles-ci ne les ont pas oublies. Des activites economiques au ralenti a Douentza, la situation s'est de nouveau degradee apres une periode de reprise de la fourniture d'electricite. La ville est plongee dans le noir depuis le lundi 23 novembre. Selon le chef d'antenne de l'energie, cette interruption est liee a une penurie de carburant. Il assure que des dispositions sont en cours pour approvisionner la localite dans les prochains jours. En attendant, les consequences se font sentir chez les petits commercants et les artisans. Oumar Ouologuem, soudeur, deplore les depenses supplementaires occasionnees par le recours aux groupes electrogenes. « Acheter regulierement du gasoil pour faire fonctionner le groupe electrogene, c'est vraiment difficile. Nous nous debrouillons comme nous pouvons. Mais avoir de l'electricite, meme si ce n'est pas 24 heures sur 24 comme auparavant, nous arrangerait beaucoup », temoigne-t-il. Pour Hawa Cisse, vendeuse de boissons traditionnelles, les coupures entraînent egalement des pertes de marchandises et de revenus. Son activite, basee notamment sur la fabrication de yaourt, de jus de gingembre et de bissap, depend fortement de la conservation au frais. « Alors, sans electricite, comment pouvons-nous nous en sortir ? », s'interroge-t-elle. Lire aussi : Bankass retrouve le courant apres des mois de coupure Dans le Nord du pays, les difficultes persistent egalement. a Menaka, les populations sont confrontees a un acces tres irregulier a l'electricite depuis plus de deux ans, selon des sources locales. En cause : la defaillance des groupes electrogenes et les difficultes d'approvisionnement en carburant. L’article Les délestages persistent dans plusieurs localités du Mali est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: JI, govt to form committee to further deliberate, implement recommendations on public relief
items.description: The federal government and Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) on Thursday agreed to form a committee to further deliberate on and implement the latter’s recommendation to improve the economy, hoping for “positive outcomes”. On Nov 11, the government and the JI had agreed on the “basic outlines” of a proposed agreement as the two sides held their 10th round of negotiations on petroleum levy relief. A final decision was expected after a meeting between Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and JI chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman, which took place on Thursday, a month after their previous one . The Rehman-led JI delegation, including Vice Emir Liaqat Baloch and other leaders, called on PM Shehbaz at the PM House in Islamabad. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, PM’s political adviser Rana Sanaullah and other government officials were also present. “We have considered the recommendations by the JI chief by all means,” PM Shehbaz said while addressing the meeting. He noted that all consultations between the two sides were held with “sincerity and honesty”. “For the betterment of the economy, it has been decided that a committee will be formed to further deliberate on and implement the recommendations by the Jamaat-i-Islami,” the premier stated. He expressed hope that the committee would result in “positive outcomes” and affirmed that the recommendations would be implemented “speedily, with sincerity and honesty”. The prime minister thanked the JI leadership and appreciated the party’s efforts to seek relief for the common citizen as fuel prices had skyrocketed due to the Middle East crisis. He also praised JI for maintaining contact with the government and discussing measures to provide maximum possible relief. PM Shehbaz recalled the government’s efforts to provide relief to the public, including allocating over Rs128 billion from the development budget soon after the US-Iran war erupted. Moreover, the government in September launched the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme to give targeted relief to two-wheelers and vehicles up to 800cc, the premier noted. He underscored that 20 million people had benefitted from the scheme. Speaking on the occasion, the JI chief said his party believed “there has been a positive development” in the talks on public relief. Appreciating the government for holding consultations over the public’s problems, Rehman emphasised that the JI would keep making efforts for further relief and engage with the government on issues facing the people. He contended that the JI had introduced a culture of peaceful resistance and still had the right to stage demonstrations to demand further relief for the public. Rehman noted that his party delegation had held more than 10 meetings with the government team. He appreciated the accessibility of the government’s fuel relief scheme, but also termed it insufficient and called for drastic measures to mitigate rising inflation. The JI has been demanding for about three months that the Centre abolish petroleum levies, as fuel prices have skyrocketed due to conflicts in the Middle East since March. The Centre and JI agreed to form committees in early September — when the latter had planned a nationwide strike — to recommend measures to reduce the levy. On Sept 20, the party launched a protest march towards Islamabad, warning that if the government failed to abolish the petroleum levy, the protest could turn into one to oust the government. On Sept 22, the JI emir said his party, whose convoy had reached Multan, was postponing its long march at the request of PM Shehbaz, who had assured the other side of a meeting to discuss the matter. When PM Shehbaz and Rehman finally met about a month later, they agreed to form a joint committee to recommend proposals for expanding the fuel relief scheme and for a phased reduction in the petroleum levy for the next budget. The committees then held multiple rounds of discussions on practical measures to provide relief to low-income citizens from petroleum prices.

items.title: Ghana targets end to raw mineral exports by 2028 – Armah-Kofi Buah
items.description: The government has said it is determined to end the exportation of raw materials by 2028, as part of efforts to accelerate domestic mineral processing to retain more value from the country’s natural resources. The Minister of Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, said the government intended to refine at least 70 per cent of artisanal and small-scale gold locally by December 2027, and increase it to 100 per cent by December 2028. He said the government was targeting local processing of at least 50 per cent of manganese and bauxite production by 2028, with the aim of processing all by 2030. “The era of exporting our minerals in raw form must give way to one in which we refine, process and manufacture our minerals at home. “We are determined to ensure that the refinery, the smelter and the steel plants are all built in the country,” Mr Buah added. Speaking at an Industrialisation Day celebration organised by the Trades Union Congress (TUC) in Accra last Tuesday, he said the policy would be supported by investments in domestic processing capacity, infrastructure and local participation to transform the mining sector and create jobs. The minister said the government had given financial commitment to the policy under the critical mineral value addition pillar of the New Economy Programme, with plans to invest $1.5 billion in domestic processing capacity for gold, manganese, bauxite and lithium. He said the investments would be complemented by the establishment of a 24-hour critical mineral processing enclave in the Western Region and the development of railway infrastructure to facilitate the transportation of minerals. Mr Buah said the Ghana Gold Board had already signed refining agreements with the Gold Coast Refinery and the Royal Ghana Gold Refinery, each with the capacity to refine up to one tonne of gold weekly He added that the Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation (GIADEC) was pursuing the development of an integrated aluminium industry, while the Ghana Integrated Iron and Steel Development Corporation (GIISDEC) was leading efforts to explore iron ore deposits in the Oti Region and other parts of the country. Local content On lithium, the minister said the Green Minerals Policy required companies to examine the domestic conversion of minerals and their by-products to ensure that more value was retained within the economy. He said the government was also seeking to strengthen local content in the mining industry by ensuring that indigenous businesses secured opportunities in procurement and supply chains. Mr Buah said the success of the policy would be measured by the capacity of local enterprises to compete for sophisticated contracts and the ability of workers to acquire transferable technical skills. He further said that the government was undertaking reforms through a new mining policy and a proposed Mining Act currently before Parliament to strengthen local participation to ensure mineral extraction delivered lasting economic benefits. Dependence The Secretary-General of the TUC, Joshua Ansah, said Africa’s continued dependence on raw mineral exports was depriving the continent of opportunities for job creation, technological development and industrial transformation. He said the continent must prioritise local mineral processing, manufacturing, technology transfer and skills development to ensure that its natural resources generate lasting economic benefits. The minister called for more transparency in mineral contracts, export pricing and beneficial ownership, stressing that illicit financial flows, tax avoidance and opaque ownership arrangements were undermining government revenues needed for development. Mr Ansah added that workers and trade unions must be recognised as strategic partners in the formulation and implementation of industrial policies.

items.title: Kanu’s release requires dialogue, not ultimatum — Tinubu’s group
items.description: By Emmanuel Iheaka The National Deputy Leader (South-East) of Renewed Hope for Greater Nigeria (RHGN), Mazi Franklin Ngoforo, has said strategic political engagement, rather than electoral ultimatums, is the way to secure the release of detained Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) leader, Nnamdi Kanu. Ngoforo was reacting to a statement by the National Chairman of Igbo Agenda Dialogue, Chief Chekwas Okorie, who warned that failure to release Kanu before the January election could trigger political backlash against President Bola Tinubu in the South-East. Okorie had suggested that the development could cost the President political support in the region. However, Ngoforo, while acknowledging Okorie as an elder statesman whose contributions to Igbo political development deserved respect, said his position should not be taken as the collective view of the Igbo people. He argued that the legitimate aspirations of the South-East for justice, equity, security and greater inclusion in Nigeria could best be achieved through diplomacy, calculated political engagement and sustained alliances with other regions and institutions of the Nigerian state. Ngoforo also credited Tinubu’s administration with interventions aimed at restoring peace in the South-East, saying the President deserved commendation for efforts to prevent further instability in the region. He noted that the circumstances surrounding Kanu’s detention predated the Tinubu administration, adding that resolving the matter required political dialogue and a commitment to national reconciliation. The RHGN leader further argued that policies and interventions by the Tinubu administration demonstrated its commitment to addressing longstanding infrastructure and economic challenges in the South-East. He cited ongoing federal highway projects, including the Enugu-Onitsha Expressway, Enugu-Port Harcourt Expressway and Enugu-Abakaliki Road, as well as other strategic transport corridors linking commercial centres across the region. He also pointed to the administration’s broader infrastructure programme, including investments in the rehabilitation of eastern transport and port infrastructure. On the economy, Ngoforo said the removal of the petroleum subsidy, foreign exchange reforms and fiscal restructuring were difficult but necessary measures aimed at strengthening government revenue, improving resource allocation, attracting investment and creating a more sustainable foundation for economic growth. He maintained that the South-East, whose economy is largely driven by commerce, manufacturing and entrepreneurship, could benefit from improved infrastructure, more efficient logistics and a stronger national economy. According to him, the revival of eastern maritime infrastructure and development of alternative trade corridors would be particularly important to businesses in Aba, Onitsha, Owerri and Enugu, whose commercial activities depend on efficient access to domestic and international markets. items.title: Afenyo-Markin accuses EOCO of abusing investigative powers over frozen funds
items.description: Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin has accused the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO) of abusing its investigative powers, questioning its handling of frozen bank accounts and the investigation involving Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah. Contributing to the closing debate on the 2027 Budget Statement in Parliament on Thursday, November 26, 2026, Afenyo-Markin argued that the conduct of the anti-graft agency was undermining confidence in the economy. He cited Article 296 of the 1992 Constitution, which governs the exercise of discretionary powers by public officers and institutions. “From the government’s own conduct and that of its agencies, particularly EOCO, this agency’s conduct in clear breach of Article 296 in itself cannot drive the economy the way it is supposed to go,” he stated. Afenyo-Markin also criticised EOCO’s investigation involving the Manhyia South MP, describing it as politically motivated and without sufficient basis. “We are all aware of the malicious prosecution being undertaken by EOCO—inspired prosecutions. Our own colleague, Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah of Manhyia South, was arrested by EOCO without cause. And today, they are prosecuting him. They are demanding documents from him 10 years back, all in the name of their so-called accountability,” he said. The MP is being investigated over allegations including money laundering, financial loss to the state and unauthorised financial transactions involving SIC Life Savings and Loans Company Limited. He has denied wrongdoing. Ghana News Agency+1 EOCO secured a High Court warrant in September 2026 authorising the MP’s arrest and the search and seizure of documents relevant to the investigation. The agency had told the court that efforts to secure his attendance had been unsuccessful. Ghana News Agency+1 The Minority Leader also questioned reports that EOCO had sought to move funds from frozen bank accounts into an account under its control while investigations were ongoing. “Why is EOCO asking a court to transfer funds from already frozen accounts into its own account when investigations are ongoing, and no criminal charges are being brought against affected persons? If the funds are already secured, what necessitates their transfer?” he asked. He further questioned the legal authority for banks to transfer customers’ funds on EOCO’s instructions without a specific court order. “Under what authority would a commercial bank, acting merely on the instructions of EOCO, transfer a client’s frozen funds into EOCO’s account without a court order? Where are these funds held? Who benefits from the accrued interest and who accounts for it?” he asked. The concerns over frozen funds come amid wider public debate about EOCO’s use of account-freezing powers in financial-crime investigations. In a separate case in March 2026, the High Court ordered the unfreezing of accounts belonging to Sesi-Edem Company Limited after finding that EOCO had acted outside its statutory mandate in the circumstances of that investigation. Ghana News Agency+1 The debate on the 2027 Budget is expected to conclude with a vote in Parliament.

items.title: Muere un marinero tras el naufragio de un buque cargado de combustible cerca de Ibiza
items.description: Un tripulante de un buque cargado de combustible ha muerto y otros seis han resultado heridos leves la madrugada de este jueves tras el naufragio del carguero, que transportaba 7.000 toneladas de carburante (más de ocho millones de litros) y se encontraba a unas 30 millas náuticas al norte de Ibiza (en torno a 40 kilómetros) y a 57 millas al este de Valencia, según fuentes gubernamentales. De los 17 tripulantes que viajaban a bordo del barco, siete de ellos han sido trasladados a Ibiza, incluido el marinero fallecido, un ciudadano turco de 46 años, que fue evacuado al Hospital Can Misses, donde se ha confirmado la muerte. Los tripulantes del carguero que navegaba con bandera de Malta son de nacionalidad india y turca, apuntan a EL PAÍS fuentes de seguridad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: L’Ukraine a détruit pour la première fois un drone à réaction avec une arme laser
items.description: Hier, mercredi 25 novembre, le conseiller du président ukrainien Zelensky, Serhii Beskrestnov, a annoncé qu'un système de défense antiaérienne laser « Blysk » avait détruit pour la première fois un drone russe à réaction de type Geran en conditions réelles. Un premier exemplaire de ce système avait été déployé plus tôt dans le mois à Kiev afin de défendre la ville face aux engins russes Publicataion de Serhii Beskrestnov sur Telegram , 25 novembre 2026.'> 1 . Selon Beskrestnov, il s'agit d'une première mondiale : jamais un drone à réaction n'avait été intercepté de cette manière. « Blysk » est un nouveau système développé par l'entreprise privée ukrainienne Carmine Sky. Son fonctionnement est similaire à celui d'autres systèmes laser, comme l'israélien Lite Beam, version allégée de l'Iron Beam, utilisé pour la première fois en conditions réelles contre des drones du Hezbollah pendant la guerre de 2023-2024. Plusieurs armées développent de tels systèmes – notamment les États-Unis, le Royaume-Uni, la France, la Chine et la Corée du Sud –, mais aucun n'avait été utilisé pour intercepter un drone à réaction, qui peut atteindre selon les versions entre 300 et 600 km/h. Le laser « Blysk » abat un drone russe à réaction Geran, novembre 2026. ©Serhii Flash / Telegram Contrairement aux systèmes traditionnels de défense antiaérienne, qui utilisent des missiles intercepteurs rares et coûteux pour détruire des drones et missiles, les armes laser fonctionnent à l'électricité. En réalité, elles ne découpent pas les ailes ou le fuselage des engins grâce à leur rayon, mais font surchauffer leurs composants internes en maintenant la tache du faisceau laser sur un point précis du drone. La puissance du laser détermine à la fois sa portée et le temps pendant lequel le faisceau doit rester fixé sur sa cible. Cette technologie pourrait doter l'Ukraine d'une arme efficace pour lutter contre les drones russes de nouvelle génération, dont la vitesse les rend très difficiles à intercepter. En octobre, la Russie a tiré plus de 4 000 drones à réaction contre l'Ukraine selon l'armée de l'air, contre environ 350 en juin. Selon l'état-major, seuls 66 % des drones à réaction ont été interceptés, contre 89 % pour les autres drones de type Shahed. Le système de défense « Blysk » reste à ce jour bien moins puissant que d'autres systèmes laser, comme l'israélien Iron Beam. Sa puissance n'est que de 4 kW, contre 100 kW pour le système israélien, et sa portée de destruction est de seulement un kilomètre – 10 fois moins que l'Iron Beam. Il est aussi très sensible aux conditions météorologiques : lors de ses premiers jours de déploiement à Kiev, la couverture nuageuse et le brouillard l'ont empêché d'engager le moindre drone « Ми захищаємо небо Києва. Тепер і лазерною зброєю ». Репортаж з позицій приватної ППО », BBC , 19 novembre 2026.'> 2 . Il faut une fraction de seconde au rayon du « Blysk » pour percer un drone léger de type FPV, mais plusieurs secondes pour venir à bout d'un Shahed, dont le fuselage est composé de plusieurs couches de matériaux. L'Ukraine a déployé plusieurs nouveaux systèmes pour défendre ses villes face aux drones russes ces derniers mois, et développe notamment un « dôme de guerre électronique », qui vise à lutter contre les Shahed à réaction pilotés à distance grâce à un « réseau maillé ». Celui-ci permet aux opérateurs russes de chercher des cibles et de guider les drones depuis la Russie. L’article L'Ukraine a détruit pour la première fois un drone à réaction avec une arme laser est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: AfCFTA: Oyedele tasks Nigeria on export competitiveness
items.description: …As NEXIM MD urges value-added exports By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has described the effective utilisation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to boost Nigeria’s export competitiveness and economic diversification as an urgent national task. Oyedele spoke at the Nigeria Export-Import Bank (NEXIM) Stakeholders’ Forum in Abuja, where he said Nigeria must strengthen its production capacity, improve the value of its exports and create better economic opportunities for its citizens. The forum was themed, “Leveraging the African Continental Free Trade Area for Enhanced Export Competitiveness and Economic Diversification.” According to the minister, access to the African market alone would not guarantee economic prosperity without the capacity to compete effectively. “Market access creates an opportunity. Our competitiveness will determine how much of it we convert into prosperity,” he said. Oyedele described AfCFTA as an opportunity to expand Nigeria’s manufacturing, agro-processing, solid minerals, creative industries and services beyond its borders. “For Nigeria, AfCFTA is a platform to take manufacturing, agro-processing, solid minerals, creative industries, and services well beyond our borders. It is not simply a commercial agreement; it is a tool for industrialisation, jobs, and shared prosperity,” he said. He called for faster financing and certification processes, as well as more efficient and predictable logistics systems to make Nigerian products competitive in African markets. The minister also urged NEXIM to play a central role in connecting the country’s export ambitions with the financing and risk-support mechanisms required to achieve them. He challenged stakeholders to take concrete steps towards positioning Nigeria as a leading player in intra-African trade, while engaging other African countries with confidence, preparation and competitive products. NEXIM MD seeks value-added exports In his remarks, the Managing Director of NEXIM, Abba Bello, said Nigeria must process more of its locally produced commodities to strengthen export competitiveness and increase foreign exchange earnings. He observed that although the country had made progress in non-oil exports, a significant proportion of its exported products remained in raw form. Bello said Nigeria’s ambition should go beyond increasing export volumes to improving the value and sophistication of goods sold in international markets. “Our ambition must extend beyond increasing export volumes. Nigeria must increase the value and sophistication of what it exports. “This requires us to process more of what we produce locally, expand our manufactured and value-added exports, deepen competitive value chains in agriculture and solid minerals, and position Nigerian services, technology and creative economy to compete across Africa and beyond,” he said. He explained that the forum was organised to explore opportunities offered by AfCFTA, particularly the prospect of making Africa the first and most accessible market for Nigerian products. According to him, since the agreement became operational in January 2021, 54 African countries have committed to a single market of about 1.4 billion people. He said the arrangement offered Nigerian businesses an opportunity to expand beyond the domestic market of about 230 million people and reach consumers across the continent. Bello cited cocoa processors in Akure, pharmaceutical manufacturers in Lagos, leather manufacturers in Kano and fashion entrepreneurs in Aba as examples of businesses that could explore markets in other African countries. He lamented that Nigeria continued to export several commodities in raw form while importing finished products that could be manufactured locally. “We produce cocoa, but import chocolate. We grow cotton, and import textiles. We produce hide and skin, and import leather products. And much of our solid minerals we export without adding value,” he said. He identified agro-processing opportunities in cocoa, sesame, cashew, cotton, ginger, shea and cassava, while noting that Nigeria’s existing capabilities in food and beverages, pharmaceuticals, building materials and consumer goods could provide a foundation for expanding manufactured exports across Africa. Quoting figures from the African Export-Import Bank, Bello said intra-African trade grew by 5.5 per cent in 2025 to approximately $213.8 billion. He said the growth demonstrated the increasing importance of trade among African countries in strengthening the continent’s resilience against external economic shocks. Cardoso calls for production-driven diversification In a message to the forum, the Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Olayemi Cardoso, said economic diversification must translate into increased production, exports and sustainable foreign exchange earnings. He said although AfCFTA provided access to a large African market, Nigeria’s ability to benefit would depend on whether local businesses could identify buyers, meet quality standards, secure financing, deliver products on time and receive payments efficiently. “To succeed under the AfCFTA, we must therefore begin with what the market demands. Export competitiveness requires the right quality, the right price, reliable delivery, and consistent adherence to standards,” he said. Cardoso also called for increased local processing, expansion of manufactured and value-added exports, stronger agricultural and solid minerals value chains, and improved competitiveness in services, technology and the creative economy. Africa must end raw materials dependence — Fashua Similarly, the Special Adviser to the President on Economic Matters in the Office of the Vice President, Dr Tope Fashua, said Africa must move away from its dependence on exporting raw materials to other parts of the world. He noted that the continent had continued to export commodities such as crude oil, cocoa, cotton and solid minerals while importing finished products, including chocolate, petrol, textiles and other manufactured goods. “For too long, Africa exported raw materials including crude oil, cocoa, cotton and solid minerals and imported chocolate, petrol, textiles and other finished goods. This cannot continue. Africa can no longer continue to be the warehouse of raw materials for the rest of the world,” he said. Fashua, however, stressed the need for African countries to build production capacity, improve product quality and meet international standards to compete effectively in global markets. He also called for stronger trade among African countries and increased participation in global commerce through the production and export of competitive finished goods. The post AfCFTA: Oyedele tasks Nigeria on export competitiveness appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nathaniel Bassey builds subsidised apartments for staff, musicians
items.description: Gospel singer Nathaniel Bassey has revealed that he has built apartments for his staff and musicians under a housing scheme designed to help them become homeowners. The singer disclosed this in an Instagram post, where he shared his excitement about seeing the beneficiaries move into their homes with their families by Christmas. Bassey said the project, which he named Love Song Apartments, was driven by his long-standing desire to help members of his team own houses. He explained that the housing scheme required the beneficiaries to contribute a significant portion of the cost, while the apartments were offered to them at highly subsidised rates. According to him, he provided a family-owned plot of land and contributed funds towards the project, while his friend, Peter Chubby of Danville Mall, partnered with him through a joint venture arrangement. The singer said construction began gradually, with the team building the apartments in phases. “One thing I realised doing this was that we used to be told musicians were not organised. But with the right guidance, they can do great things. They have committed to this. See, you never know what you can do until you try,” he wrote. Bassey said he was particularly delighted at the prospect of seeing the beneficiaries settle into their fully owned apartments with their children enjoying the play area provided within the estate. He described the project as an expression of his belief that leadership should involve extending opportunities and blessings to others. “This is never to brag. I’m not that kind of person. But sometimes, people need to see these things to know God is faithful,” he added. The singer also disclosed that the housing project was only its first phase, expressing hope that more apartments would be developed in the future. He said he hoped to share the knowledge and experience gained from the initiative with other creatives and musicians in the Christian community to encourage them to pursue similar projects. Bassey further emphasised the importance of leaders carrying their team members along as they achieve personal success, saying that a leader should not be the only one enjoying the benefits of progress. “Finally, as a leader, if you are the only one sharing testimonies, after a while, those around you will soon be despondent. Make sure as God lifts you, you carry them along,” he wrote. The post Nathaniel Bassey builds subsidised apartments for staff, musicians appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: À Ziguinchor, des femmes sonnent la mobilisation pour dire stop aux VBG
items.description: Une caravane de sensibilisation a fait escale ce jeudi 26 novembre 2026, à Colobane, à Ziguinchor, dans le cadre du lancement de la campagne des « 16 jours d’activisme » contre les violences basées sur le genre (Vbg). Portée par le réseau « Siggil Jiggen », cette mobilisation régionale et sous-régionale entend briser le silence, encourager la dénonciation et faire de la lutte contre toutes les formes de violences une responsabilité collective. ZIGUINCHOR – À l’occasion de ladite caravane, des femmes venues de plusieurs régions du Sénégal et de pays voisins ont, à l'étape de Ziguinchor, uni leurs voix pour appeler à une mobilisation plus forte contre ce fléau. À cet effet, le message se veut sans équivoque : les violences basées sur le genre ne doivent plus être passées sous silence. Pour la secrétaire générale de la plateforme « Usoforal » et membre de son conseil d’administration, Mame Ngom Faye, cette étape à Ziguinchor traduit une volonté de rapprocher la campagne des populations. « Nous sommes très heureuses, en tant que membres du réseau Siggil Jiggen, d’avoir accueilli cette caravane dont le point de chute a été le quartier de Colobane, à Ziguinchor. Cette initiative marque le lancement des 16 jours d’activisme contre les violences basées sur le genre. Pour cette cinquième édition, le réseau a fait le choix de décentraliser ses activités en organisant la caravane dans la région de Ziguinchor », a expliqué Mme Faye. La mobilisation a largement dépassé les frontières de la région. Des participantes venues de Sédhiou, Kédougou et Kolda, mais également de Mauritanie, de Gambie et de Guinée, ont pris part à cette initiative. Une présence qui donne davantage de portée au plaidoyer et renforce la nécessité de briser le silence autour des violences. Pour la responsable d’Usoforal, dénoncer ne signifie pas exposer l’intimité des victimes, mais créer les conditions pour que ces violences disparaissent à jamais. « Le maître-mot reste la dénonciation. Il ne s’agit pas de dévoiler des secrets ou d’exposer publiquement des situations privées, mais de faire en sorte que les violences basées sur le genre deviennent un vieux souvenir », a-t-elle plaidé. Organisée chaque année, la campagne des 16 jours d’activisme est aussi l’occasion de rappeler que les violences ne concernent pas uniquement les femmes. Elles peuvent être physiques, économiques ou verbales et toucher aussi bien les femmes que les hommes. « Nous espérons que cette année, nous pourrons enfin dire : « Dafa doy » (ça suffit). Chacun doit comprendre que la dénonciation est la seule voie pour combattre toutes les formes de violences, quels que soient leurs auteurs et leurs victimes », a-t-elle souligné. Des viols passés sous silence Poursuivant, son plaidoyer, Mme Faye a insisté sur les violences verbales, souvent banalisées, mais dont les conséquences peuvent être profondes. « Dans notre société, la dignité occupe une place importante. Pourtant, les paroles blessantes peuvent porter gravement atteinte à cette dignité et détruire chez une personne des choses qu’il sera parfois très difficile de reconstruire », a-t-elle averti. Évoquant également les viols commis sur les femmes, les jeunes filles et même les enfants en bas âge, elle a appelé les victimes et leurs proches à sortir du silence. Restant sur cette même dynamique, Mame Ngom Faye a rappelé l’existence de dispositifs d’accompagnement, notamment le numéro vert gratuit 116, les points focaux dans les quartiers et les « Bajenu Gox ». Ces mécanismes permettent aux victimes de signaler les faits dans la discrétion et de bénéficier d'un accompagnement adapté. Au-delà de la caravane, l'ambition est de faire de la dénonciation un réflexe collectif et de rappeler qu'aucune considération sociale ou culturelle ne saurait justifier les violences. Pour les actrices mobilisées, le véritable succès de ces 16 jours sera de parvenir à faire reculer durablement le silence et l'impunité. Gaustin DIATTA (Correspondant)

items.title: Control without confiscation: How Ghana can own the chain from pit to port, and turn raw exports into jobs
items.description: Ghana earned about 31 billion dollars from exports in 2025, a record, yet gold alone supplied 63.1 per cent of the total, up from 38.5 per cent in 2004, and gold, cocoa and oil together supplied about 86 per cent. Behind those figures sits a young and underemployed workforce. The Ghana Statistical Service reports that unemployment among 15 to 35-year-olds averaged 21.9 per cent in the first three quarters of 2025, against 12.8 per cent nationally. The Chamber of Mines says its member companies directly employed 13,819 people. A pit does not employ a generation. A refinery, a smelter and a factory might. The loudest answer in Ghana’s resource debate is to nationalise everything. The evidence points to something harder: control of the chain, yes; blanket nationalisation, no. And where the chain needs capital Ghana does not have, the question is not whether to accept foreign money but who holds the decisions. That difference decides whether this becomes a revolution in jobs or a repeat of the country’s own history. What Ghana owns, and what it actually collects The law already says the minerals belong to the people. Article 257(6) of the Constitution vests every mineral in the President on behalf of, and in trust for, the people, and Parliament must ratify every mining lease. The weakness is collection. The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates that Ghana’s 2025 mining revenue was 1.6 billion dollars, 11.9 per cent of roughly 13.4 billion dollars of sector value added, against an average of 60.9 per cent for Botswana across 2019 to 2023. Its 6.56 billion dollar gap is a rough comparison rather than an audit, but the direction is hard to dispute. The state’s 10 per cent free carried interest under section 43 of Act 703 has not closed it, because the costs it is carried for are recovered out of its dividends, and the Natural Resource Governance Institute’s 2019 reading of company disclosures found little dividend income from it. The sharpest leak is in the sector Ghanaians already own. Small-scale mining is reserved by Act 703 for Ghanaian citizens. In 2025 it produced 3.11 million ounces, 52.4 per cent of national output, and about 10.8 billion dollars of exports. The IFS found no royalties recorded from that segment, and the Natural Resource Governance Institute reports that fewer than 10 per cent of small-scale operators pay PAYE and corporate income tax. Ownership, in other words, is not the same as benefit. The state is already moving, and the bills are arriving Policy has shifted fast. The sliding-scale royalty in L.I. 2517 runs from 5 per cent at 1,900 dollars an ounce to 12 per cent at 4,500, and first-half 2026 royalty receipts of GH¢5.39 billion almost matched the whole of 2025. From July, large miners must sell 30 per cent of output to GoldBod in doré, up from 20 per cent. The government says raw small-scale gold exports end by December 2028, and a phased ban on raw ore exports is targeted for 2030. Yet state trading carries its own costs. The Bank of Ghana reportedly posted an operating loss of about GH¢15.6 billion in 2025, partly reflecting the cost of its gold purchase programme. Official gold reserves fell from 33 tonnes to 24.4 tonnes in the year to June 2026, and the Governor acknowledged that gold shipments slowed in August, shortly before a ban on exporting unrefined doré took effect on 1 September. Oil shows both the promise and the delay. Parliament ratified extensions of the Jubilee and TEN licences to 2040 in February 2026, with Jubilee gas priced at an escalating 2.50 dollars per mmbtu. The state petroleum company gains a further 10 per cent interest in both fields, but only from July 2036. That is a genuine revisiting of a deal, and also a decade of waiting. If a larger stake is worth having, it is worth asking why it begins in 2036, when today’s graduates will be in their thirties. What happened when the state tried before Ghana has run this experiment. In 1961 the State Gold Mining Corporation took over five mines, and by 1972 the state held 55 per cent of Ashanti Goldfields. Gold output fell from more than 900,000 ounces in the early 1960s to about 280,000 in 1983, and Ghana missed most of the price boom of the 1970s. Today’s warnings are no less real. Mali’s standoff with Barrick over Loulo-Gounkoto reportedly cost the company about 430 million dollars in settlement fees and an estimated 1.9 billion dollars in lost revenue; Mali lost taxes and royalties during the suspension, and its gold output fell 19 per cent in 2025. Closer to home, the state already controls cocoa marketing through COCOBOD, yet industry reporting puts installed processing capacity at around 500,000 tonnes with utilisation below half, and the 50 per cent local processing mandate only begins in 2026/27. The state-owned Tema Oil Refinery struggled for nearly eight years to process the country’s crude. Official statements describe the June 2026 delivery of Jubilee crude to the Sentuo refinery as the first such cargo refined at home, fifteen years after first oil, and Sentuo is Chinese-owned, even as fuel makes up 26 per cent of imports. State ownership is a tool, not a guarantee. Everything Ghana ships raw Gold, cocoa and oil dominate the headlines, but the same pattern runs through almost everything else Ghana sells. Ghana mined about 5.2 million tonnes of manganese in 2025, and the Nsuta mine has shipped ore since 1916. The ore still leaves at around 27 per cent manganese for the plants of its Chinese parent, which owns 90 per cent of the mining company. Ghana also mined about 2 million tonnes of bauxite, and all of it left raw. The Volta Aluminium Company smelter in Tema, which runs at roughly 23 per cent of capacity, imports all of its alumina. Ghana sells the ingredient and buys it back half-made, while GIADEC puts the country’s bauxite reserves at around 920 million tonnes. Farm commodities tell the same story. Government figures put annual output at about 250,000 tonnes of cashew, 145,000 tonnes of rubber and 130,000 tonnes of shea, with roughly 95, 95 and 90 per cent exported raw. A 2026 study by the French non-profit Nitidæ found that Ghana processed only about 15,000 tonnes of its 262,000-tonne cashew crop in 2025, under 6 per cent, while raw exports of around 444,000 tonnes included nuts smuggled in from neighbours. It also found business interest rates near 20 per cent in Ghana against about 9 per cent in Vietnam. Raw shea nuts earned 177.8 million dollars in 2025, slightly more than the 174.3 million from shea oil. Iron tells a more hopeful story: about 80 per cent of domestic iron rods are made locally, largely from scrap, yet a scrap export ban dating from 1980 has leaked for decades, and steel makers cite high electricity costs. Lithium, iron ore and diamonds sit on the same 2030 list. Quarries and the quiet mines Quarries look unglamorous, but they are the cheapest place to practise ownership. Capital needs are modest, the product is sold at home, and demand follows every road, bridge and housing estate. Commercial quarry operators told the Minerals Commission in February that granite deposits should be demarcated against encroachment, that quarrying should be reserved for Ghanaians, and that unauthorised foreign involvement should end. They also alleged that traditional leaders are not receiving their royalties from the Minerals Development Fund. That makes quarries a question of enforcement and fairness, not new law. Cement shows what a missing mineral costs. Ghana is Africa’s largest importer of clinker, spending close to 500 million dollars a year, and the cement makers’ chamber says local limestone is unsuitable for clinker. The answer is invention: a 110 million dollar plant using limestone and calcined clay, both found here, is expected by its owners to replace about 400,000 tonnes of clinker imports annually. Ownership can also mean owning the technology to work with the rocks the country has. What the great powers actually do The assumption that powerful nations simply shut foreigners out does not survive the facts, and the real picture is more useful. China’s 2024 Negative List prohibits foreign investment in the exploration, mining and beneficiation of rare earths, radioactive minerals and tungsten, yet it welcomes foreign capital across much of the rest of mining. Russia does not ban foreigners from strategic subsoil; it demands state approval once an investor reaches control thresholds, 25 per cent for deposits of federal significance. The United States, the supposed champion of markets, has bought in: the Pentagon took roughly 15 per cent of MP Materials with a 110 dollar per kilogram price floor on neodymium-praseodymium, and a 10 per cent stake in Trilogy Metals followed. Norway owns 67 per cent of Equinor and holds direct licence interests through Petoro, with the cash flow banked in its sovereign fund, yet foreign operators such as ConocoPhillips drill beside the state. Saudi Arabia reached full ownership of Aramco in 1980 by buying out the American owners in stages, 25 per cent in 1973 and 60 per cent in 1974, rather than confiscating. Botswana co-owns Debswana equally with De Beers, and its state seller will take up to half of the output over the new ten-year contract. Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020 and built an industry, but foreign, mainly Chinese, capital built the smelters. The pattern is consistent: sovereignty means holding the decision, not supplying every dollar. None of these is a model to copy wholesale, since each fits its own geology and institutions. Own it, partner or rent it: the FDI question Both slogans fail. Relying on foreign direct investment as the default has left decisions elsewhere: the manganese refinery depends on the Chinese parent that has long shipped the raw ore, the first Jubilee crude refined at home went to a foreign-owned plant, and the Ewoyaa lithium developer now faces a 210 million dollar takeover by China’s Huayou after a lease that took from October 2023 to March 2026 to ratify. But refusing foreign capital outright would fail on arithmetic. Investment promotion estimates put an alumina refinery and a smelter at about 1.5 billion dollars each, and Gold Fields has proposed a Tarkwa renewal backed by about 6 billion dollars. A sorting rule is more honest than a slogan. Own outright where capital needs are modest, and the market is at home: quarries, small-scale gold refining and assaying, shea, cashew and rubber processing, scrap and steel finishing. Own the majority, with partners, where capital is heavy, but the chain is strategic: alumina, aluminium, manganese refining, local oil refining. License on strict terms where risk and technology are foreign: deep-water oil and large gold. Domestic savings can do more than is often assumed. Pension assets reached GH¢108.88 billion at the end of 2025, yet private pension funds still held 64.5 per cent of their portfolios in government securities, and regulators raised the cap on alternative assets from 10 to 25 per cent in 2024. Patient domestic capital, properly governed, should lead the minority-to-majority stakes in processing, with foreign partners bringing technology, markets and the rest of the money on Ghana’s terms. Where the jobs really are The arithmetic of employment explains why processing matters more than ownership percentages. Extraction is capital intensive, and the contrast between 13,819 direct mining jobs and youth unemployment near 22 per cent shows it. The Chamber also estimates 207,285 indirect and induced jobs, though that is a modelled multiplier, not a headcount. Work tends to multiply downstream, in assay laboratories, refineries, smelters, jewellery, steel and component manufacturing, and in the engineering firms that serve them. The President has projected 10,000 new steel jobs from the scrap export ban, a projection worth testing. Those jobs appear only if power is reliable, finance is patient, and training matches the work. Without those conditions, a ban on raw exports produces a stranded plant, which is why the 2030 target needs milestones and a delivery plan, not just a date. A viable path What follows comes from first principles rather than from anyone’s template. First, own the chokepoints: the sale, assay and refining of all gold, and the tenure, data and tendering of every licence, because bargaining power sits there. Second, make equity earn. A free stake that pays nothing is decoration. Equity should be priced, staged and governed by dividend and cost-recovery rules written into each lease, and every lease should go to open tender with beneficial owners disclosed. A lease awarded, even by tender, to a contractor owned by a relative of the head of state, as happened at Damang, may be lawful and still corrode trust. Nationalism that enriches the well-connected is privatisation by another name. Third, collect where the state already controls. Because GoldBod holds the exclusive right to buy small-scale gold, royalty and tax can be deducted at the point of purchase, closing the leak the IFS describes without opening a single new mine. Fourth, save the windfall. Gold hit a record above 5,500 dollars an ounce in January and has since fallen more than 30 per cent, and a legal rule that banks revenue above a base-case price protects the budget when the price turns, as it always does. Fifth, sequence the bans. Pair every raw export prohibition with power, finance and a named processor, so the ban follows capacity rather than preceding it. Sixth, bargain together: Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire have renewed calls for more local cocoa processing, and a buyer finds it harder to play two sellers against each other than one. The honest counter-case The Chamber of Mines says its members returned 70.8 per cent of 2024 mineral revenue to Ghana, and warns that insecure tenure would starve long-term investment, and the jobs that depend on it. DLA Piper counted 32 resource disputes at the World Bank’s arbitration centre in the first ten months of 2025, a ten-year high. These warnings deserve respect, because capital remembers who tears up contracts. But the Chamber’s figure is a broader measure than state revenue, set beside the GH¢17.68 billion in fiscal payments its own report records, and the IFS finding comes from an independent body. The public deserves audited, published numbers to settle the argument. The test arrives in April 2027, when the Tarkwa leases expire, and Gold Fields seeks a 25-year renewal. Whether the state renews, renegotiates or re-tenders, the process should be open, the fiscal terms published and the outcome judged on jobs, local processing and revenue, not on who holds office. Ghana does not lack resources. It lacks leverage over what happens after they leave the ground. In a country where more than one in five young people in the labour force is jobless, the question is no longer whether to take control but how to do it without repeating 1983. The viable answer is sovereignty over the chokepoints, honest equity, open tenders, strict collection, and processing at home, owned by Ghanaians where possible and shared on Ghana’s terms where necessary. Anything less keeps Ghana exporting ounces, tonnes and kernels, and importing opportunity. Anything cruder risks exporting its graduates instead. – Dominic Senayah is an International Relations professional and policy analyst based in England, specialising in African political economy, humanitarian governance, and migration diplomacy. He holds an MA in International Relations from the UK and writes on trade policy, institutional reform, and Ghana–UK relations for audiences across Africa, the United Kingdom, and the wider Global South.
