items.title: Measles, MAHA, and the Future of Disease in America
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Updated at 9:35 a.m. ET on November 26, 2026 The measles are back. The U.S. achieved measles-elimination status back in 2000 and then lost it earlier this month. To date, there have been more than 40 outbreaks and 5,800 cases since the year began, according to the CDC data—a significant jump from the 2,289 confirmed cases last year. Such an outbreak is exactly the sort of thing lawmakers who questioned Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s anti-vaccine activism during his confirmation hearings had been worried about. “Frankly, you frighten people,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said at the time, before urging Kennedy to promise “never to say vaccines aren’t medically safe when they in fact are.” Since the measles-elimination status was removed, Kennedy has argued that Americans need to work to rebuild trust in vaccines. As the Make America Healthy Again movement comes face-to-face with the dangers of abjuring scientific consensus, my colleague Tom Bartlett joins me to discuss an outstanding question: Where do we go from here? The following is a transcript of the episode: Tom Bartlett: Most people in this country are in favor of vaccination—Democrats, Republicans. We’re actually not that polarized on that issue. What we have is a very vocal group of people, including Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who have been pushing this contrarian and erroneous message about the dangers of vaccines for a long time. But if you get to the point where you have parents sort of forgoing normal childhood immunization, yeah, we should be worried. [ Music ] Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to talk about measles and MAHA. During his confirmation hearing to become the secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services in 2025, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.: I wanna thank President Trump for entrusting me to deliver on his promise to make America healthy again. Harris: But last week, after nearly three decades, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States has lost its measles-elimination status. Measles was eliminated back in 2000 because people were getting their shots, but in recent years, vaccination rates have fallen as misinformation about their safety has proliferated. When the elimination status was removed, Kennedy Jr. said, quote, “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust.” But many scientists and doctors argue Kennedy, a noted vaccine skeptic, is a large part of the reason why that trust was broken in the first place. What does it mean that measles are back? And where does the movement to make America healthy again go from here? My colleague Tom Bartlett joins me to discuss. Let’s get to questions. Tom, thank you so much for joining me. Bartlett: Thanks, Adam. Harris: I wanna start with a basic question. How did we get here? What does it mean that the U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status? Bartlett: In technical terms, it means that we’ve had at least 12 months where a single strain has been transmitted throughout the country. And so you have this essentially unbroken stretch where people have been getting the measles. So that’s sort of the technical definition. But I mean, I think measles is now—it was ruled eliminated in 2000, which means there were still sporadic outbreaks, but it was basically under control. And so losing that elimination status is really a sign that it’s really no longer in control, and that there’s this work to be done. In terms of how we got here, I think the key thing that people point to is pandemic disruption in vaccination schedules and areas where that vaccination rate among kindergartners fell below 95 percent, which is the herd-immunity threshold. So that’s kind of the basics of why we’re here. Harris: I guess how big of a deal is it that we’ve lost the status? If it’s sort of moving from sporadic to a sort of continuous strain of infections, is this, like, COVID-size, or what’s the scale that we’re thinking of here? Bartlett: So right now, these infections have been mostly confined to severely undervaccinated communities. So it’s a lot of Mennonite communities and Amish communities. And for the most part, that’s where it stayed. And so, are we looking at COVID-wide outbreaks? I think the short answer is no, but we also just don’t know where this ends, how much bigger this gets. We do have undervaccinated areas of the country that aren’t predominantly Mennonite or Amish. They haven’t, for the most part, been affected significantly. But I think we don’t know where this ends. And then just in general, it’s a sign that something needs to be done, a vaccination push or something, because it’s no longer eliminated. We thought we were moving toward eradication, which would be: We don’t have any outbreaks at all, even sporadic ones. And this is really a big step back. So it’s really a sign that we’ve taken a step back, and that’s not what we would hope to do from a public-health point of view. Harris: I think most people don’t necessarily have a context for measles at this point, or if they do, it’s so far removed, and we can talk about it in terms of the numbers, but there is a real sort of human impact to this. These are families who are experiencing the loss of loved ones. You’ve done a lot of reporting in these communities. You’ve talked to some of these families. Can you sort of humanize this a little bit for folks? What are these families going through? Bartlett: Yeah, you’re right. It’s not something that most of us sort of under a certain age have any experience. It’s also not something that most doctors have encountered, which has been an issue too, because how do they recognize cases? It’s not something they’re used to seeing normally. But yeah, for those families, I’ve talked to families—Amish families and Mennonite families—you know, sort of the obvious: It’s frightening. They’ll have children; often these families are quite large, and so all the children will be sick at the same time. Measles is among the most communicable diseases that we have. It spreads very easily and very quickly, and so an entire family or entire community can become infected. And so, yeah, frightening when you have several children who are ill. I’ve certainly talked to families who had a couple of kids who were extremely ill, trouble breathing, you know, dehydrated. It affects people differently, and in some cases it is fairly mild. In other cases, it’s really severe, and it’s sort of hard to know exactly how it’s gonna happen. But certainly, these are families that are dealing with tremendous grief. Losing a child is, you know, I think no greater grief. And I think a lot of them are—they were caught off-guard by this. I mean, they didn’t see this coming. It hadn’t been a problem in their communities, really, either for a long time. Harris: Speaking of they didn’t see this coming , there was one family you spoke to who didn’t even know that their child had become a sort of national headline after their death. I imagine, you were able to get more information from the person who was doing the autopsy than the parents were, it seemed. How did they sort of navigate that sort of information gap? Bartlett: When I spoke to them—this is a family in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, which is really one of the counties that’s been hardest hit. It has a large Amish community. That disease has really gone throughout that community, and really everyone that family knew, or seemingly everyone they knew, had been affected. When I spoke to them in August, they were certainly frustrated that they had been getting so little information from the state, and what became a national controversy about the death of their child that they were pretty much entirely unaware of. And they didn’t realize it had become this source of controversy between the health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the governor of Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro. It was certainly my impression that they weren’t getting sort of clear communication about what was going on and what the results of the autopsy were on their child. Harris: One of the things that we’ve kind of seen surfacing is this idea of comorbidities, right? It was similar with COVID, where it’s like, Oh, they didn’t die of COVID. They died of excess fluid in their lungs , or, They died from pneumonia that was exacerbated here . Similarly with measles, right? It opens children up to greater susceptibilities to different viruses. And so where someone might say, It was measles , and the other person might say, It was the spleen , or someone might say, It was measle s, someone else might say, It was pneumonia . How is that conversation, the comorbidities piece of this, affecting the measles dialogue at the moment? Bartlett: I think that’s been one of the most interesting things in terms of how people are taking this. So there’s a certain group of people who wanna say, Well, if you have these comorbidities, or if you’re vulnerable, you’re immunocompromised, and you die from the measles, that, quote-unquote, “didn’t count.” But this is the reason we sort of do universal vaccination, because we have people who are going to be more vulnerable to diseases, and we want to keep them from getting it. So I mean, that part of the debate, I think, has been sort of misleading and frustrating. And it’s not just children. So one of the deaths in Pennsylvania was a mother, and she did have a number of comorbidities. And no doubt, that factored into her death. But when I was speaking to the coroner there, he said this was a mother who was regularly making dinner for her children, was living a normal life, and was dealing with the issues that she had, and she was unvaccinated for measles. She got the measles and she died. Comorbidities don’t make those deaths any less of a tragedy, nor do they undermine the case for universal vaccination. To my mind, they strengthen the case for universal vaccination. Harris: I wanna talk about RFK Jr. a bit here and his role. He said that measles was beginning to spread in the U.S. before his term as secretary, but the spread has gotten worse since then. So what has his response been to the outbreak and also to the elimination status? Bartlett: I think his response has been confusing, honestly. I mean, he has said, a range of things that are contradictory. A good thing to note in the background that’s just simply true is that he is a longtime anti-vaccine activist. When you look at things that he said before becoming health secretary, where he has said, It’s basically misinformation that measles is deadly , or he said that w e don’t have proof that the vaccine is safe or effective, which we do. So I mean, that’s the background. But he’s also sort of touted things, touted vitamin A, which can be a treatment in some cases but is in no way a substitute for vaccination. You know, a very mixed message and sort of not what public-health officials would certainly hope that someone in his position would say. Harris: And I guess with the strength of the anti-vax movement in the U.S., are there other diseases on the horizon that folks should be worried about? If it’s not just the sort of skepticism about measles but also the skepticism about these other vaccines? Bartlett: Yeah, it’s a totally reasonable question. I’ve spent a lot of time talking to people who are very much in that anti-vaccine world and who would say they don’t want their children vaccinated for any disease, including, say, polio. That’s still a relatively small part of the population. A thing generally to note is most people in this country are in favor of vaccination—Democrats, Republicans. We’re actually not that polarized on that issue. What we have is a very vocal group of people, including Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who have been pushing this contrarian and erroneous message about the dangers of vaccines for a long time. But I think that’s a thing to be concerned about if you get to the point where you have parents sort of forgoing normal childhood immunization, yeah. Should be worried. [ Music ] Harris: When we come back, we’re going to talk about that very vocal group of people and where they go from here. [ Break ] Harris: So we’ve been talking about disease and vaccine skepticism, sort of a tenet of the MAHA movement, which some argue helped propel Trump back into the White House in 2024. But MAHA is also associated with nutrition, exercise, wanting to reform food and agricultural systems. So two years after the 2024 election, where does the MAHA movement stand, and what’s its sort of relationship to the president at the moment? Bartlett: If you listen to Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and some of his close supporters, they will talk about its successes. They haven’t achieved many of the things that they hoped to achieve, and they’ve also had a number of setbacks over sort of key issues. And so, one thing to say sort of politically is: MAHA had been touted as potentially an enormous influence on the midterms, and they really weren’t. Two of the candidates they really pushed were Zach Lahn in Iowa and Ken Paxton in Texas. Both of those candidates lost. The race that they really spent a lot of money on as a primary race was against Bill Cassidy, who’s a Republican. And so MAHA hasn’t been this force for Republicans politically that it was sort of touted as. In terms of what its achievements have been, they will say they’ve raised issues that are important to the American public. But in terms of solid accomplishments, they will point to things like the limits on SNAP purchases for soda, which is sort of state-by-state, or they will point to a change in dietary guidelines. But there haven’t been, sort of, the solid wins for MAHA that they had hoped. Harris: What were their reasons for backing these specific candidates? For backing Paxton or for sort of running against Cassidy? Were there sort of ideological goals that they were after there? Bartlett: Paxton has been willing to sort of make announcements about going after sort of industries that MAHA is against, so sort of questioning vaccines or the food industry or things like that. Cassidy was really targeted seemingly because he, even though he voted to confirm Kennedy, had pushed back in a number of instances on things that Kennedy wanted to do and questioned him on vaccines. Cassidy’s a physician, has expertise in this area. And so I think that was the reason there. Harris: Are there priorities that MAHA has had to sort of leave on the table? I know one of the big things was sort of getting the big money out of medicine, out of health care. But it seems that’s one of those priorities that they’ve sort of shelved a little bit. So are there other priorities that they’ve sort of left on the table? Bartlett: Their biggest defeat, I would say, this year, at least in terms of what MAHA activists wanted, was around the herbicide glyphosate. And they really wanted action limiting glyphosate. In fact, Trump back in February issued an executive order really, under the Defense Production Act, sort of protecting the supply of glyphosate. That was a huge— Harris: Sorry. When you say “glyphosate,” can you just explain that to those of us who aren’t scientists? Bartlett: Yeah, of course. So glyphosate is a really commonly used weed killer, and so there are concerns about whether that’s linked to cancer or not. There’s some dispute about how strong those links are. And so that’s been a long-standing goal of Kennedy’s, even before he became health secretary, to sort of oppose glyphosate, and that had been one of the things that activists had hoped he would do. And so that hasn’t happened. So that’s one thing that’s been left on the table. Really, there’s a whole slew of issues that MAHA has talked about that really haven’t come to fruition. Harris: We’ve seen a sort of fracturing of the MAHA movement based on the fact that they aren’t able to get some of those priorities that they were hoping for, the sort of return on investments. Is that fracturing of the MAHA movement real? Bartlett: Yeah, I think that fracturing of the MAHA movement is real. It was always an uneasy coalition. The thing that’s happened in recent months is a lot of the people who were Kennedy’s strongest supporters have been unhappy with the progress that he’s made, including, in fact, some of his anti-vaccine supporters, who wanted him to take action to pull COVID vaccines from the market. That was the thing they really wanted. That hasn’t happened, so a lot of those people are disappointed. So yeah, I mean, I think it has fractured. But I think it was just always this sort of bizarre coalition. Harris: Yeah, it’s just that now the fault lines are more recognizable. Bartlett: That’s right. Harris: You had a story over the weekend about Secretary Kennedy urging the White House for a new definition of ultra-processed foods , but there’s been some pushback from the White House. Why is that new definition important? Bartlett: Yeah, it’s a story that Michael Scherer and I have been working on. For months, Kennedy has promised a federal definition of ultra-processed foods. That matters because once you have a definition, you could potentially move forward on putting labels on foods that were ultra-processed, but you have to have that definition first. He’s been promising that for months. It appears to have been delayed for quite some time, and now the word is that it may be forthcoming, and it may happen. That would certainly be maybe the biggest accomplishment for MAHA because it would potentially set the table for different kinds of dietary guidelines, warnings. And that’s a move that a lot of nutritionists that I talk to are excited about. They think it’s a good first step toward warning people about ultra-processed foods, which have been linked to obesity and diabetes and cancer and a range of other chronic diseases. So that would be a big deal for Kennedy. Harris: And what has the pushback been? Bartlett: Kennedy has wanted this definition for ultra-processed foods. He’s wanted this for months. He said much earlier this year on Joe Rogan that the definition would be coming out very soon. And there’s been, apparently sort of behind the scenes, there have been delays in the administration about when exactly this definition could come out, and I think that’s been a source of frustration. One of Kennedy’s sort of top allies, Calley Means, quit, in part he says, because this definition had been, in his view, slow-rolled. And so, that behind-the-scenes wrangling has been, I think, a frustration to Kennedy and a frustration to some MAHA supporters. Harris: Just thinking about the next couple of years, we know that Democrats will have control of Congress come January. Is there any indication that Secretary Kennedy is among those who they’re looking to investigate or potentially impeach? Bartlett: Yeah, that’s a good question. I think it’s gonna be really interesting to see what Democrats do. Annie Andrews, who’s the senator-elect from South Carolina, who’s a pediatrician, really said she was inspired in large part to run because of Kennedy and has talked about holding him accountable. And so, whether that’s something that Congress does I think is gonna be interesting to see. Certainly the possibility of impeachment seems unlikely. But maybe, who knows? Harris: Secretary Kennedy celebrated Stephen Miller’s recent ascent to chief of staff at the White House following the midterms. What is the nature of that relationship? And does it sort of solidify these ties between MAGA and MAHA? Bartlett: I think MAHA supporters had been buoyed by Stephen Miller becoming chief of staff. There was at least a perception that his predecessor, Susie Wiles, was holding back some of the priorities of MAHA. And there’s the feeling—Kennedy has said this, and others have suggested this—that Miller is going to be a closer ally, specifically potentially on vaccines. Miller has echoed some of the things Kennedy has said and some of the things that Trump said about pumping shots into babies and we don’t know the long-term effects and this is a medical travesty . It’s worth saying that we actually have studied the long-term effects of these vaccines and that’s, I think, false. But it makes him seem like a kindred spirit to Kennedy, and so that’s gonna be really interesting. Whether Kennedy is in fact more empowered in this regime than he was in the prior one is TBD. Harris: Even after this Trump administration, there are still vaccine skeptics in the nation. And herd immunity is a large part of why you need folks to get vaccinated. I guess what are you hearing about what it actually will take to rebuild that trust, even beyond this Trump administration? Bartlett: One of the consequences of having Kennedy as health secretary is a lot of his ideas and frankly his misinformation has this megaphone, and has gotten to people that might not have been aware of it before. I think we don’t know what the effect of that will be. I think it’s something that, probably, public-health officials are gonna be attempting to clean up for a long time. And we don’t know whether, they’ll say, the loss of elimination status or the concern around measles—is that going to spur more parents to go get their children vaccinated? In some of these hard-hit communities, that has in fact been the effect, which is encouraging. But I think we just don’t know how long it’s gonna take to rebuild that trust, and some of it’s going to start with having a public-health leader who offers sort of clear messaging that’s in line with what we know from the science. Harris: Well, Tom, thank you so much for your time and for helping us understand all of this better. Bartlett: Thanks, Adam. [ Music ] Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pisoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you wanna support this work and the work of my colleagues here at The Atlantic , you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Until next time, I’m Adam Harris. This article original identified Senator Sheldon Whitehouse as the senator of Idaho, he is in fact the senator of Rhode Island.

items.title: The Scandinavian Compromise
items.description: We live in a divided nation, and for at least the next two years, we’re going to have a divided government, with one party in control of Congress and the other in control of the White House. But never fear: I am here to bring us together. I think I’ve found a model that I believe will give people on the right and the left what they want. And, unusually for a former Wall Street Journal editorial page writer, I’m looking to Scandinavia for inspiration. As Brink Lindsey argues in his book The Permanent Problem , the two big challenges we face are inclusion and dynamism. First, inclusion. It’s possible to get distracted by the current arguments about the exact nature of America’s class divide. Progressives emphasize how much wealth is going to the top one percent. People like me emphasize that the top 20 percent has created a caste system separating the highly educated, who rig everything to their benefit, from everybody else, who are left with the scraps. The truth is that both kinds of inequality are terrible. Great nations decline when they become grossly unequal, and America is staring that possibility straight in the face. Second, dynamism. Yes, it’s true that over the course of this century the American economy has enormously outperformed the economies of Germany, France, Britain, and Japan. But you get no prizes for besting those geezers. The fact is that for the past 50 years, America’s economic growth and productivity numbers have been sluggish and disappointing. This loss of economic dynamism has retarded wage growth, led to fiscal crises, and contributed to a decline in social mobility. In her forthcoming book, Reviving the American Dream , the Brookings Institution economist Isabel Sawhill notes that if America had sustained the productivity growth levels we enjoyed from 1948 to 1973, and if wages had kept pace with productivity, then the average annual earnings for a 25-to-54-year-old worker would be close to $180,000 a year. Instead, we’re living in a country in which the average wage is less than $70,000 a year. The psychological effect of these two crises is devastating—loss of trust, pessimism, alienation, class resentment, and pervasive economic insecurity. Historically, responsibility for these two problems has been divided between the major parties. Republicans were the party of dynamism, emphasizing tax cuts, competition, and deregulation. Democrats were the party of inclusion, emphasizing redistribution, public subsidies, and social insurance. Republicans argued that big welfare states lead to stagnation and torpor. Democrats countered that unfettered capitalism leads to concentration of wealth and exploitation. Then along came Donald Trump, who disagreed with both of those frameworks. He offered a worldview based on protection, claiming that tariffs and immigration barriers would produce a revival of manufacturing. But Trump’s economic formula has manifestly failed—there are scarcely more manufacturing jobs now than when he first glided down the golden escalator. [ Teresa Ghilarducci: The welfare state: A terrible name for an essential system ] America no longer has a party that offers a full-throated case for economic growth. Instead, the Republican Party resembles an intellectual black hole as it approaches the post-Trump era. The Democratic Party, meanwhile, is being pulled leftward by a bunch of young socialists who champion tried-and-failed policies such as rent control, putting me in mind of that old Richard Weaver maxim: The problem with the younger generation is that they haven’t read the minutes to the last meeting . Here’s why I think the Scandinavians offer us a road map out of this morass: They’re less likely to have our mental categories in their heads. They don’t assume that inclusion and dynamism are at war with each other. They don’t believe you have to choose between capitalism and welfare. Scandinavians have the kind of big supportive welfare systems that make lefties pant in admiration, but most Scandinavians see no contradiction between these systems and aggressive free-market policies. Every year, the libertarian Cato Institute ranks nations in its Human Freedom Index. The Cato ranking system rewards nations for their rule of law, low regulations, free trade, smallish government, property rights, and freedom of religion and expression. In the Cato freedom index, Denmark, Finland, and Sweden all rank higher than the United States. Some people think of the Scandinavian nations as progressive nirvanas. The story is more complicated than that. For example, the Swedish economist Andreas Bergh divides his country’s economic history into a series of eras. First came the period of 1870 to 1970, when Sweden rose from abject poverty and became one of the richest nations in Europe. There were a lot of causes for this ascent, but my favorite is the Bildung educational policies that the Swedes adopted in the 19th century. They understood that if their kids were going to contribute to an industrial economy, they would need complex inner lives. They would need to understand complex systems. They would have to take more responsibility for the people and national organizations around them. The Bildung approach to education was a human-capital grand slam. Sweden’s second economic era, according to Bergh, lasted from 1970 to 1995. The country took its newfound wealth and veered left, increasing the tax burden and the size of government, while gradually transferring corporate ownership to funds connected with organized labor. This is the version of Sweden often valorized on the left, but it’s not the end of the story. In the 1990s, Swedes across the political spectrum realized: Holy Crap! Our economy is tanking, and we won’t have the tax revenues to fund our welfare state! That led to a series of free-market reforms—cutting marginal tax rates, reducing taxes on capital, and increasing competition in a series of formerly regulated sectors, including telecom, electricity, aviation, postal services, and financial markets. Bergh emphasizes that these reforms were not adopted in a ruthlessly partisan manner. Social Democrats acknowledged the need for a dynamic capitalist economy, while conservatives accepted the welfare state. The country rebuilt a competitive market economy while shoring up its social-insurance system. Today, if you look across Northern Europe, you will see a bunch of policies the Democratic Socialists of America would hate: countries with no wealth tax or minimum wage, that embrace school vouchers or low corporate taxes. The Fraser Institute ranks the progressivity of the tax systems in each of the OECD nations. The United States has the most-progressive tax system in the developed world. The Scandinavian nations are clustered around the bottom. [ Derek Thompson: A simple plan to solve all of America’s problems ] If you scan the region, you see a smorgasbord of arrangements that combine dynamism and inclusion. In Denmark, firing people is relatively easy, giving the labor market much-needed flexibility, but unemployed workers receive both substantial income protection and assistance with retraining and job placement. In Sweden, the government generously funds education, but parents have the freedom to choose which school their kids go to, and schools, including for-profit ones, compete for students. Sweden also reduced corporate-tax rates while widening the tax burden through consumption taxes. The Nordic nations pursue full employment—they want people behaving like good capitalists and workers—but they advance that cause with ideas that sound lefty in the American context, such as universal child care and parental leave. These nations have both flexible labor markets and strong unions. I don’t think that it would work to copy and paste Scandinavian arrangements directly onto American soil. These are (or, at least, used to be) cohesive, high-trust, communal societies with cultures very different from our own. Their institutions work pretty well, while our state capacity is in sharp decline. Their middle classes are willing to pay higher taxes in exchange for public support, but it’s not clear the American middle classes are willing to do that. Denmark has one of the most restrictive immigration policies in Western Europe, which would not be appropriate for a nation of immigrants such as the United States. Plus, in the past several years, many Scandinavian nations have turned the dial too far over to the inclusion side, at the cost of economic dynamism. Growth and productivity rates have begun falling alarmingly. Nonetheless, those tall peoples from up north offer a general approach that is worth learning from. They teach us that it is possible to build a productive workforce within a generous welfare state; to provide economic security for individuals while nurturing capitalist creative destruction; to secure people from some of the disruptions of economic modernization, while still encouraging that modernization. Furthermore, they teach us that there is a difference between protecting people and protecting jobs. You can give somebody economic security without locking them into one specific employer. There is likewise a difference between who pays for a service and who performs it. You can have governments generously pay for services and allow private firms to compete to offer them. The Scandinavians also show the limits of our conception of freedom. In America, we tend to understand freedom as freedom from the state, but how free are you really, if you are free from Uncle Sam but you live under the thumb of that manager you detest at Sam’s Club and you can’t afford to switch jobs? So this is the trade-off that I’m proposing: Progressives, you’re going to have to live with a world that is friendlier to corporations and billionaires than you might like, but you get those welfare policies you’ve been talking about for decades. Conservatives, you’re going to have to live with a bigger government than you might like, but you get flexible labor markets, free trade, low taxes on investment, and productive workers. This model has been sitting there for decades. At periodic intervals, a writer pops up to argue that we should adopt it. But political partisans have refused to embrace it because they have succumbed to the idiot’s primary delusion: Someday, the other half of the country is going to be totally defeated, and my side is going to get everything we want . Meanwhile, the intellectuals have been immobilized by their resentments. The lefties are immobilized by their resentments toward all those vulgar B-school types who looked down on them in college. The righties are immobilized by their resentment toward all those “woke” sociology majors who think that they can salvage their disappointing lives by seizing political power. [ Mike Solana: The abundance delusion ] But I stumble toward the end of the Trump era, having reached a few conclusions. American capitalism is not working for many middle-class American families. At the same time, the sort of policies that American progressives support have sent European countries such as France, Italy, and even Germany into what looks like long-term stagnation and decline. We need a new approach that goes hard on both ends: hard on free-market dynamism and hard on economic security. It’s like going to a Chinese restaurant in which you pick a lot of dishes from column A and also a lot from column B and you fit them together on the same plate—it makes for a more satisfying meal. If I were ordering off the menu, on the inclusion side, I’d support child tax credits and wage subsidies such as the earned-income tax credit. I’d accede to the child-care and family-leave policies that my lefty friends think are important. I’d support stronger unions to defend worker interests. On the dynamism side, I’d support every human-capital policy you can lay your hands on—school reforms such as the kind that have powered the test-score surge in many Republican states; charter schools; better worker training across their lifespan. I’d support ways to increase public support for scientific research significantly. Over time, I’ve become less impressed by the power of tax cuts to spur economic dynamism, but I’ve become more impressed with the power of deregulation. The abundance movement offers many ways to deregulate home construction (though its adherents don’t like it when you use the word “deregulate”). In their book, The Captured Economy , Brink Lindsey and Steven Teles of the Niskanen Center show just how rife our economy is with “regulatory capture”—the many ways that private companies co-opt state power in order to reduce competition. As they write, “State action, by suppressing and misdirecting entrepreneurship and competition, has rendered our economy less innovative and dynamic as well as less fair.” To pay for all of this, I’d support a tax on consumption rather than a tax on savings and investment. As some economists have long joked, Democrats will come to love consumption taxes when they realize how much revenue they raise, and Republicans will love them when they realize how regressive they are. (It’s also possible to design them so they are not regressive.) For decades, progressives have talked a lot about equality and conservatives have talked a lot about freedom, but these days, I’d put the emphasis on agency. How can we create a society in which people have more control over their lives, more opportunity to venture forth and build things for themselves? Nobody has any clue what AI is going to do to our economy over the next few decades, so I’d be in favor of empowering people to come up with their own adaptations, their own new forms of labor, and their own new forms of economic organization. I want an economic system that infuses people with a spirit of daring, exploration, curiosity, ambition, and aspiration. For that, you need both a secure base and an open field to explore. In his book Mass Flourishing , the Nobel laureate Edmund Phelps writes that “the good life requires the intellectual growth that comes from actively engaging the world and the moral growth that comes from creating and exploring in the face of great uncertainty.” Today, like Phelps, I sense that Americans are suffering from an uncharacteristic loss of national nerve. The spirit of venturesomeness is being replaced by a spirit of fear and loss aversion. I want an economy that will encourage people to venture out into the new, to lead brave and satisfying lives. And to get that economy, I’m willing to live with compromises that I wouldn’t have considered a decade ago.

items.title: ‘‘Mektoub’’ ou anatomie d’une Tunisie qui ne sait plus aimer
items.description: Dans son livre numérique ‘‘Mektoub, mon amour. Pourquoi les Tunisiens ne savent plus tomber amoureux’’ , Karim Ben Aziza retrace cinquante ans de bouleversements amoureux à travers quatorze archétypes, témoins d’une société tunisienne tiraillée entre liberté individuelle, héritage familial et quête d’intimité. «Autrefois, le destin réunissait deux êtres. Aujourd’hui, les algorithmes multiplient les rencontres, sans nécessairement rapprocher les cœurs. Entre le poids des traditions et la promesse de la modernité, la Tunisie traverse une profonde mutation sentimentale» , note l’auteur. Il ajoute : «Au-delà des histoires de cœur, ce livre interroge notre époque : avons-nous réellement gagné la liberté d’aimer, ou simplement multiplié les raisons de ne plus nous choisir ?» Il constate, par ailleurs, que les nouveaux codes de l’attirance algorithmique, on trouve plus difficilement sa place et on découvre pourquoi trouver l’amour n’est plus aussi simple qu’avant. L’article ‘‘Mektoub’’ ou anatomie d’une Tunisie qui ne sait plus aimer est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Réhabilitation du Transgabonais : l’emprunt de 113 milliards de FCFA auprès l’AFD en quête du feu vert parlementaire
items.description: Parmi les six textes présentés à l'Assemblée nationale le 25 novembre par le ministre de l'Économie, figure une demande d'autorisation d’emprunt de plus de 113 milliards de FCFA auprès de l'Agence française de développement. Comme expliqué lors de l'adoption du projet de texte en Conseil des ministres sept mois plus tôt, ces ressources sont destinées à la réhabilitation du Transgabonais. 203 millions d'euros, soit 133,2 milliards de FCFA : l'enveloppe AFD-Union européenne pour la modernisation du Transgabonais a été adopté lors du Conseil des ministres du 30 avril 2026. © D.R. Le réseau ferroviaire gabonais pourrait bénéficier d'un nouveau financement extérieur. Le ministre de l'Économie, des Finances, de la Dette et des Participations, Thierry Minko, a transmis aux députés un projet de texte adopté en Conseil des ministres le 30 avril 2026 autorisant l'État à contracter un emprunt de plus de 113 milliards de francs CFA auprès de l'Agence française de développement (AFD). Ce financement, qui sera accompagné d'une subvention de 30 millions d'euros accordée par l'Union européenne (UE) et gérée par l'AFD, est destiné à la réhabilitation du Transgabonais, infrastructure essentielle au transport des marchandises et des voyageurs dans le pays. Une infrastructure stratégique à remettre à niveau Long d'environ 650 kilomètres, le Transgabonais constitue un maillon central de l'économie nationale. Il assure notamment l'acheminement du manganèse depuis les bassins miniers du Haut-Ogooué vers le port d'Owendo. Sa disponibilité et sa fiabilité conditionnent donc directement les performances du secteur minier, mais aussi la mobilité des populations et les échanges économiques entre les différentes localités desservies. Le financement envisagé s'inscrit dans la volonté des autorités de renforcer les capacités de cette infrastructure et d'améliorer ses conditions d'exploitation. Une autorisation parlementaire attendue Le projet présenté aux députés vise à obtenir l'autorisation législative nécessaire à la conclusion de cet emprunt. Lors de la présentation, une interrogation a toutefois été soulevée sur la nature de la procédure : s'agit-il d'une autorisation préalable ou d'une régularisation d'un engagement déjà intervenu ? Cette distinction n'est pas anodine au regard du contrôle parlementaire de l'endettement public. L'enjeu est désormais de connaître le calendrier des décaissements, les conditions financières du prêt et la programmation précise des travaux. Dans un contexte de contraintes budgétaires, le recours aux financements extérieurs peut permettre d'accélérer les investissements. Il impose néanmoins une exigence de résultats : les ressources mobilisées devront se traduire par une amélioration mesurable de la qualité du service ferroviaire. L’article Réhabilitation du Transgabonais : l’emprunt de 113 milliards de FCFA auprès l'AFD en quête du feu vert parlementaire est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: PM Shehbaz launches ‘Mehfooz Dawa’ app to combat counterfeit and substandard medicines
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday launched the “Mehfooz Dawa” app to prevent the circulation of counterfeit and substandard medicines, calling it “a major milestone” and saying the initiative would help restore public confidence in the healthcare system. The prime minister said education and healthcare facilities should be equally accessible to every citizen and stressed that the federal and provincial governments must work together to ensure the availability of affordable, quality medicines. The prime minister was speaking at the launch ceremony of the Ministry of National Health Services’ “Mehfooz Dawa” app, which was developed to track medicines. Federal Minister for National Health Services Mustafa Kamal and Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) Chief Executive Officer Dr Obaidullah also addressed the event. Addressing the ceremony, PM Shehbaz hailed the development, describing it as “an extremely magnificent moment” for Pakistan’s medical facilities. He recalled a 2012 incident at the Punjab Institute of Cardiology in which counterfeit medication was blamed for the deaths of more than 100 patients. At the time, DRAP had maintained that the medication was genuine; however, international testing found that the medicine administered to the patients was intended to treat malaria. He called for “learning from the past and preparing ourselves” for the future. The prime minister lauded Kamal’s efforts and directed his ministry to work with the IT and Information ministries to raise public awareness about the app. “History will remember this step in golden words,” the premier remarked. Noting the application’s mechanism, the premier said it was an “excellent intervention”. “But the real point is that, to make medicines affordable for the common man, their prices should be in line with what ordinary people can afford,” he said, stressing that obtaining medicines was a “huge challenge” for millions of people in the country. The prime minister further said: “The founding principle of our policies should be that health and education are equal for everyone and no one should have to go begging and pleading at anyone’s door.” Speaking at the ceremony, the health minister said the application had been developed with the aim of “protecting innocent lives”. He also noted a “lack of trust” among the public when it came to obtaining medicines. He praised the pharmaceutical industry’s cooperation, adding that building a database covering around 92,000 medicines and involving more than 700 companies had been an “uphill task”. Dr Obaidullah explained that the app sought to address three issues: counterfeit medicines, shortages and quality compliance. The application has three features — medicine verification, complaints and shortage reporting, he said. By scanning a medicine’s batch number, which would then be checked against a database, users can verify whether the product is authentic, he said. The application will display a green screen if the medicine is genuine and a red screen if it is counterfeit. If a medicine is found to be counterfeit, consumers will have the option to lodge a complaint. He added that DRAP’s database, which is linked to the application, contains details of around 92,000 medicines. Users will also be able to report medicine shortages through the application, the DRAP chief said. He added that the government had provided citizens with “protected public health” through the application. Earlier this month, Drap’s spokesperson Sajid Shah had said the track-and-trace system became operational on October 9. The idea of introducing a barcode system was first proposed in 2015. It was approved by the federal cabinet in 2017; however, bureaucratic delays prevented its implementation. Earlier, Kamal, taking notice of the delay, announced that the system would be launched as soon as possible. Earlier this year, Drap had set October 1 as the cut-off date for launching the barcode system to curb the sale of counterfeit and expired medicines and eradicate black marketing. Shah said the Ministry of National Health Services was “dedicated” to ensuring that citizens had access to high-quality and effective therapeutic products.

items.title: SOGUIPAH : la PCA Kanny Soumano fait le point sur les décisions du CA et les perspectives de relance
items.description: À l’issue de la session extraordinaire du conseil d’administration de la Société guinéenne de palmier à huile et d’hévéa (SOGUIPAH SA), tenue le 25 novembre 2026 dans un réceptif hôtelier de Conakry, sa présidente, la présidente du Conseil d’Administration (PCA) Kanny Soumano, est revenue sur les principales décisions adoptées. Examen des états financiers des trois derniers exercices, validation de trois projets de financement, plan d’urgence de relance sur deux ans et suivi des anciennes résolutions : elle détaille les mesures engagées pour redresser l’entreprise. Interview… Journaliste : Quel est l’objectif de cette session extraordinaire du conseil d’administration ? Kanny Soumano : Nous avons convoqué une session extraordinaire ce 25 novembre 2026. L’objectif était de passer en revue et d’examiner les états financiers des exercices 2023, 2024 et 2025. Les administrateurs ont examiné les états présentés par le commissaire aux comptes, sous la coordination de Monsieur le directeur général. Je tiens d'abord à le féliciter pour tout le travail accompli. Aujourd'hui, au niveau du conseil d'administration (CA), nous disposons d'une situation plus ou moins claire sur la vie de la SOGUIPAH. Nous avons formulé des recommandations et mis en place un comité de suivi et d'accompagnement de la direction générale pour finaliser ces états financiers, qui seront bientôt certifiés. Nous avons également examiné les projets de financement en cours et validé l'ensemble du travail présenté. Je crois que nous avons validé trois projets de financement et donné notre accord à la direction générale pour poursuivre leur finalisation avec les partenaires. Par ailleurs, nous avons examiné le plan d'urgence de relance de la SOGUIPAH, qui s'articule autour de trois phases : la stabilisation, le redressement et la transformation. Ce plan devrait permettre à l'entreprise de se relancer effectivement au cours des deux prochaines années. Nous avons aussi passé en revue le suivi des recommandations et des résolutions issues des précédentes sessions du conseil d'administration. Il y en avait environ 33. Après examen, nous avons constaté que 16 résolutions ont été entièrement exécutées. Les autres sont en cours de réalisation et feront également l'objet d'un suivi du conseil d'administration auprès de la direction générale. Quel regard portez-vous sur la situation actuelle de la SOGUIPAH ? Comme je viens de le dire, depuis notre nomination, nous avons constaté que la SOGUIPAH est aujourd'hui dans une situation de crise. Avec les états financiers présentés au conseil, nous sommes désormais plus à l'aise pour parler de la situation de l'entreprise, parce que nous disposons d'éléments factuels et de justificatifs sur sa gestion et son fonctionnement. Madame, après cette rencontre, quelle sera la prochaine étape ? La prochaine étape, c'est ce que je viens d'évoquer : nous avons déjà mis en place une commission technique chargée d'accompagner la direction générale jusqu'à la certification des états financiers des trois derniers exercices, 2023, 2024 et 2025. Nous allons également assurer le suivi du plan d'urgence que nous venons de valider, lequel porte sur deux ans. Ce plan est assorti d'un plan stratégique que nous avions validé en début d'année. Quelles sont vos attentes à l'égard de la direction générale ? Notre attente est que la direction générale poursuive son engagement en faveur du redressement de la SOGUIPAH. Propos recueillis par Ousmane CAMARA L’article SOGUIPAH : la PCA Kanny Soumano fait le point sur les décisions du CA et les perspectives de relance est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Centrale/Coopération décentralisée : Une délégation de la Région Grand Est en visite de travail à Sokodé
items.description: Sokodé, 26 nov. (ATOP) – En mission de suivi-évaluation de ses projets dans la région Centrale, une délégation de la Région Grand Est (France), a échangé avec les responsables du Conseil régional de la Centrale, le mercredi 25 novembre à Sokodé. Cette visite s’inscrit dans le cadre de la coopération décentralisée entre les deux régions. La délégation de la Région Grand Est est composée de la vice-présidente chargée du Transfrontalier, de l’Europe et des Relations internationales, Brigitte Torloting, et du directeur du Rayonnement transfrontalier international et de l’Europe, Jean-Baptiste Cuzin. M. Cuzin exposant le partenariat entre les deux régions La rencontre a permis aux deux parties de partager leurs expériences sur l’organisation de leurs territoires, les processus de régionalisation, la décentralisation et la gouvernance locale. Elle a également été l’occasion de présenter les deux régions sous l’angle de l’organisation, de compétences, d’atouts et de stratégies de développement. L’historique et les perspectives de la coopération entre les deux collectivités ont également été exposés, donnant lieu à des échanges constructifs. Le vice-président du Conseil régional de la Centrale, Amadou Yérima Mashoud, a salué l’engagement des autorités de la Région Grand Est, leur disponibilité et volonté constante de dialogue. Il a également remercié leur opérateur technique, Gescod-Togo, pour son accompagnement et son rôle déterminant dans l’animation et le renforcement des relations entre les deux collectivités. Pour lui, cette rencontre constitue une occasion de renouveler les engagements et de nourrir les ambitions communes afin d’ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives de collaboration au bénéfice des populations respectives. Il a insisté sur la nécessité de consolider les initiatives porteuses de résultats et de promouvoir des actions concrètes, durables et mutuellement bénéfiques, au service du développement des territoires et du bien-être de leurs habitants. La vice-présidente de la Région Grand Est, Brigitte Torloting, s’est réjouie de la qualité des échanges qui contribuent au renforcement du partenariat entre les deux régions. Elle a précisé que la mission vise à apprécier concrètement, sur le terrain, les réalisations issues de cette coopération et à recueillir les attentes des bénéficiaires. « C’est aussi une fierté d’apprendre que ce qui a été mis en œuvre dans chaque domaine a eu un impact très positif sur les bénéficiaires », a-t-elle confié. Les participants En marge de cette rencontre, la délégation de la Région Grand Est s’est également entretenue avec les membres de l’Association des femmes élues locales de la région Centrale (AFELoRCET). La Région Grand Est est engagée dans une coopération décentralisée avec la région Centrale depuis 1987. Ce partenariat est axé sur le développement durable des deux territoires. Pour assurer le pilotage et la mise en œuvre des actions, la Région Grand Est s’appuie sur une délégation au Togo dénommée Gescod. Basée à Sokodé, celle-ci est dirigée par Ouronilé Adam Daouda. ATOP/TAA/MEK/JK

items.title: US clears SpaceX to launch up to 1 million orbital data-center satellites
items.description: The Trump administration authorised Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Wednesday to launch up to one million satellites as part of its plan to build data centres in space, raising concerns from some experts. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said SpaceX’s Starmind constellation would “process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth.” The company’s authorisation runs until 2040, according to a document published on the FCC’s website. “America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement, using Trump’s moniker for artificial intelligence. He added that data centres would be “essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI.” Projects for orbiting data centres have multiplied over the past year. Alongside SpaceX and its Starmind constellation, Google is pursuing its own initiative under the codename “ Suncatcher ,” while Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin has submitted an application to the FCC for its “ Project Sunrise .” Several startups are also in the race, including Starcloud, which successfully operated an advanced processor known as a GPU aboard a satellite in late 2025. Google also reached that milestone in October. SpaceX has the advantage of having its own rockets that have already completed hundreds of missions. In August, Musk promised a first SpaceX satellite launch into orbit in the fourth quarter of 2027 and a ramp-up in 2028. The company has struck a deal with Nvidia, which will supply its latest-generation Vera Rubin processors, specially designed to operate in space. ‘Disheartened and dismayed’ Most space-based data centre projects have a similar architecture: a constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO), positioned close together to ensure reliable connections between them. Starmind’s satellites will communicate with those already in orbit as part of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network, which will then relay the data to Earth. Other competing networks plan to receive data directly from Earth and send it back using lasers. But experts have warned of technical obstacles, as well as environmental concerns. Unresolved technical challenges include processors’ ability to withstand the high levels of radiation in space. Observers also point to the difficulty of withstanding extreme temperatures or avoiding damage from space debris and micrometeorites. The American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by Wednesday’s decision. “The proposed constellation would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the AAS said in a statement. It noted that the constellation “involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects,” meaning the satellites would “be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky.” “Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the nonprofit group Earthjustice, said in a statement. However, there are numerous advantages to locating a data centre in space over building one on Earth. Among those, a satellite in what is known as a sun-synchronous orbit can capture solar energy continuously and with eight times the efficiency of its ground-based equivalent. SpaceX made its stock market debut in June, raising about $85.7 billion.

L’avocat du Sénégal, l’Espagnol Juan de Dios Crespo, a réagi dans les médias espagnols. Celui que l’on surnomme « champion du TAS » a également évoqué l’éventuel recours des Marocains auprès du Tribunal fédéral suisse. Juan de Dios Crespo, le « champion du TAS », a encore frappé. Considéré comme l’un des avocats les plus redoutés en matière de droit sportif, l’Espagnol peut ajouter une nouvelle victoire à son tableau de chasse. L’homme de loi, interrogé sur un recours du Maroc auprès du Tribunal fédéral suisse, a évoqué les chances de la Fédération royale marocaine de football (FRMF), qu’il juge infimes. « Une décision du TAS ne peut se réfuter qu’en très peu d’occasions. La probabilité que le Maroc inverse la situation est de 0,00001 %. Ce n’est pas impossible, mais ça l’est pratiquement », assure-t-il d’abord. Juan de Dios Crespo a ensuite pointé du doigt l’erreur stratégique des Lions de l’Atlas lors de cette finale. « Les joueurs du Maroc sont restés sur la pelouse pour gagner sur le terrain. Si Brahim n’avait pas tiré ce penalty et que le Maroc avait refusé le retour du Sénégal, le Maroc aurait gagné 3-0. Leur volonté de gagner sur le terrain a pris le pas sur le fait qu’ils avaient déjà la victoire dans la poche. » O.B.N

items.title: Major economies balk at new US tariffs over 'unfair' trade
items.description: Major economies from China to the European Union hit out at proposed US tariffs after Washington concluded its months-long probe into alleged excess production, potentially opening a new phase in trade tensions with both allies and foes alike. The new tolls, which follow an investigation launched days after the Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump’s previous duties, range up to 20 per cent and face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January. The levies target some of the United States’ largest trading partners, with China, the EU, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam in the crosshairs. A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the proposals sought to take existing trade deals into account. China is among those facing a 20 per cent tariff, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing. “China understands that we’re going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding,” he told US broadcaster CNBC , adding that Washington was offering China exemptions on around $30 billion of goods. Beijing hit out at the proposed tariffs on Thursday, warning that it could take “necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.” Chinese commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong told a regular briefing that citing “overcapacity” — mass production at a loss to flood overseas markets and undercut local rivals — as a reason to impose tariffs was a “pretext for protectionism.” He urged Washington “to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation.” ‘Real concern’ Along with other countries, Japan denied having excessive production. “Japan does not have any non-market policy practices or structural excess production capacity … It is regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced in spite of this,” top government spokesman Minoru Kihara said. The EU said it rejected the premise of the new tariffs and expected the United States to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said. And Singapore said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals, and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing. Vietnam also faces a 20pc tariff; Cambodia and Indonesia 18pc; and India 17pc, according to the US trade representative’s office. The EU, South Korea and Taiwan, which have signed trade deals with the United States, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15pc. In a separate announcement, the trade representative also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns. The Brazilian president’s office called the measures “unacceptable” and said Brasilia would “not yield to this type of threat”. Trump’s tariffs have targeted Washington’s friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in the country. Overcapacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement and chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said. ‘Hollowing out’ The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now more likely to pass on expenses to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living. Affordability was a key issue in this month’s US midterm elections , which saw Trump’s Republican Party swept out of power in both chambers of Congress by Democrats. The announcement came as data showed the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge at a three-year high in October, adding to pressure to hike interest rates. Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected the production probe to be among “the most important” actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and “never get turned off, even if there’s no demand.” This could potentially lead to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a “hollowing out” of US manufacturing, he added. While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact. The new levies will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said. In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour. For economies facing both the forced labour and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack up and the higher rate would prevail, the US official said.

items.title: Pour les États-Unis, l’Algérie est le « partenaire sécuritaire le plus compétent » au Sahel
items.description: Mark Schapiro, le chargé d’affaires de l'ambassade des États-Unis à Alger, s'exprime dans un média algérien pour la première fois depuis son arrivée en Algérie en mars dernier. Schapiro a accordé un entretien au quotidien gouvernemental El Moudjahid dans lequel il a abordé plusieurs sujets liés à la relation bilatérale. Des extraits de l'entretien ont été diffusés par le journal sur les réseaux sociaux. Lawrence : personne ne s'attendait à « autant d'élan et autant d'énergie » M. Schapiro a été interrogé sur le lien né pendant la Coupe du monde 2026 entre l’Algérie et les habitants de la ville américaine de Lawrence, dont une délégation vient de séjourner en Algérie à l’invitation du président Abdelmadjid Tebboune. Le chargé d’affaires a dit que tout le monde s'attendait à ce que le stage de l’équipe d’Algérie à Lawrence donne lieu à « une histoire positive », mais pas à « autant d'élan et autant d'énergie ». « La vraie image réside dans les liens humains, lorsque les populations apprennent à se connaître », a-t-il souligné, non sans saluer le gouvernement algérien et le président Tebboune pour avoir invité la délégation américaine à visiter l’Algérie. « L’Algérie est le partenaire le plus compétent de la région du Sahel » Schapiro a aussi parlé de ta situation au Sahel et du rôle de l'Algérie dans la stabilité régionale. « Il est clair pour nous que l’Algérie est le partenaire sécuritaire le plus compétent de la région du Sahel, une région volatile et instable marquée par des trafics divers. L’Algérie a accompli un travail remarquable pour surveiller et sécuriser ses propres frontières », a-t-il reconnu. « Dans la mesure où l’Algérie peut exporter ce savoir-faire au reste de la région, nous voulons voir si nous pouvons encore plus développer cela », a ajouté le diplomate américain. La même vision à l'égard des importateurs qui veulent « se faire de l'argent rapidement » Mark Schapiro s'est attardé sur le volet économique, relevant des similitudes dans les politiques menées actuellement par les deux pays. « Nous comprenons la vision du président Tebboune pour l'économie. Pourquoi ? Parce que cela ressemble beaucoup à notre politique. Nous voulons aussi la production locale aux États-Unis. Nous sommes parfois sceptiques à l'égard des importateurs qui veulent venir se faire de l'argent rapidement », a-t-il expliqué. Décrivant le marché algérien, le chargé d'affaires américain a estimé qu’il s’agit d’un marché « à haut effort et à haute récompense ». Baladna : fascination pour les vaches qui traversent l’océan, des États-Unis vers l’Algérie « Nous sommes également très enthousiastes à l'égard du projet Baladna », a-t-il fait savoir, évoquant notamment l’importation de vaches américaines pour cette ferme géante que l'Algérie réalise dans le désert en partenariat avec les Qataris. « Tout le monde semble fasciné par la façon dont les vaches montent dans les avions et comment elles voyagent pour traverser un océan, des États-Unis vers l'Algérie », a indiqué Mark Schapiro. Des Américains concourent pour des licences dans les télécoms en Algérie Le diplomate américain a aussi fait une confidence concernant l’activité des entreprises de son pays en Algérie. Selon lui, des entreprises concourent actuellement pour des appels d'offres et des licences dans le secteur des télécommunications. Il s'est gardé toutefois de citer les noms des entreprises concernées. L’article Pour les États-Unis, l'Algérie est le « partenaire sécuritaire le plus compétent » au Sahel est apparu en premier sur TSA .
